But it attached a condition that will decide whether that custody is permanent or temporary: it must end the day the father remarries or enters into a live-in relationship, at which point custody passes to the mother. Until then, the mother gets free access to the child and a one week stay with her every two months, wherever she is located. The bench described the mother's underlying concern, about the child's upbringing and welfare, as reasonable, and it was this concern that the condition was designed to answer.
why_it_matters: Indian courts increasingly attach conditions to custody orders tied to a parent's remarriage or live-in relationship, treating it as a welfare factor rather than a moral one. This order confirms that practice at the High Court level and shows that such conditions can be imposed even in a habeas corpus proceeding converted into a custody dispute, giving family law practitioners a fresh precedent on how far courts will go to future-proof a custody award against a parent's later personal choices.
title: MP High Court Gives Father Custody of Daughter, Conditional on Not Remarrying or Entering a Live-In Relationship
meta_description: MP High Court grants a father custody of his daughter but orders it to shift to the mother if he remarries or enters a live-in relationship.
card_tip: In a custody dispute raised through habeas corpus, expect the High Court to decide custody once the child is produced, and negotiate any remarriage or live-in condition into the order itself.

case_name: Shivshakti Enterprises v. Commissioner of Customs
citation: Bombay High Court, order dated 31 August 2026
holding_summary: Shivshakti Enterprises imported two consignments of roasted areca nuts and, as the law requires for any food item entering India, had them examined by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. FSSAI issued a no-objection certificate confirming the goods met food safety standards. That should ordinarily have been the end of the regulatory gatekeeping on the food-safety side, clearing the way for the goods to be released once customs duty and classification formalities were sorted out. Customs did not see it that way. It sent its own samples to the Central Revenue Control Laboratory for testing and, even after that testing was done, permitted only a provisional release of the consignments, and only on condition that the importer execute a bond and furnish a bank guarantee of Rs 40 lakh. The department's position was that an FSSAI no-objection certificate settles food safety but says nothing about the correct customs tariff classification of the goods, so Customs remained free to hold the consignments pending its own satisfaction on that separate question. The importer took the matter to the Bombay High Court, where a Division Bench of Justices M.S. Karnik and Sandesh D. Patil found the issue squarely covered by the court's own recent decision in NBG International Private Limited v. Union of India, a case that had dealt with an identical stand-off over imported roasted areca nuts earlier in the year. In NBG International, the court had held that once FSSAI's authorised officers examine samples and issue a no-objection certificate confirming compliance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, Customs cannot simply disregard that finding in favour of a contrary report from its own revenue laboratory.
why_it_matters: Food importers frequently find consignments held up at the port even after FSSAI clears them, with Customs citing its own laboratory results or unresolved tariff classification questions to justify continued detention and onerous bank guarantee conditions. This ruling, following closely on the Bombay High Court's NBG International decision, reinforces that FSSAI clearance is determinative on food safety and that Customs cannot use a parallel classification dispute as a pretext to keep goods detained on a security deposit.
title: Customs Cannot Keep Withholding Goods for Fresh Testing Once FSSAI Has Cleared Them: Bombay High Court
meta_description: Bombay High Court orders release of imported areca nuts without a bank guarantee, holding Customs cannot override an FSSAI no-objection certificate.
card_tip: Where Customs detains a food consignment or demands a bank guarantee after FSSAI clearance, cite NBG International and this ruling to argue the detention cannot stand.

case_name: Trendset Jayabheri Projects LLP & Ors. v. Neelima Vanguru
citation: T.A. No. 35 of 2024, Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal
holding_summary: A flat buyer in the Trendset Jayabheri Elevate project in Hyderabad complained to the Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority about two things: her occupancy certificate arrived late, and the clubhouse in the project did not match what had been sanctioned and disclosed when she bought her flat. The authority found against the promoter and imposed a penalty of Rs 27.5 lakh. Trendset Jayabheri Projects LLP and two associated landowners appealed to the Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, arguing the penalty was disproportionate to what they called a minor and cost-neutral construction variation. The underlying facts, once laid out, made the promoter's characterisation harder to sustain. The clubhouse had originally been sanctioned and uploaded to the RERA website in 2017 as Ground plus two floors. The occupancy certificate the promoter eventually obtained, however, referred to a building permit showing Ground plus three upper floors, meaning an entire additional floor had been added to the amenities block at some point without the revised sanction ever being disclosed to allottees or uploaded to the regulatory portal as the law requires. Two defences anchored the promoter's appeal. First, that the extra floor cost allottees nothing and was, in the scheme of a large residential project, a trivial deviation not worth a penalty of this size. Second, that the complaint was not maintainable at all, because an earlier compensation proceeding between the same parties had already dealt with related grievances, and allowing this complaint to proceed would amount to relitigating settled ground.
why_it_matters: Promoters often treat changes to shared amenities such as clubhouses as a lesser category of deviation that does not require the same disclosure and consent process as changes to saleable units. This ruling confirms that Sections 11(3) and 14 of the RERA Act apply equally to amenity-block construction, and that a promoter cannot defeat a penalty by characterising an undisclosed extra floor as trivial or cost-neutral, strengthening allottees' hand in disputes over unsanctioned project changes.
title: Promoter Cannot Dismiss an Undisclosed Clubhouse Floor as Trivial: Telangana REAT Upholds Rs 27.5 Lakh Penalty
meta_description: Telangana REAT upholds a Rs 27.5 lakh penalty on a promoter for an undisclosed clubhouse floor added without two-thirds allottee consent.
card_tip: When a promoter alters a sanctioned plan, including common amenities, check if the revised plan was uploaded to the RERA website and allottee consent obtained before accepting a triviality defence.

case_name: In re: Scheme of Amalgamation between Tata Steel Limited and Rujuvalika Investments Limited
citation: C.P. (CAA) 69/MB/2026 connected with C.A. (CAA) 162/MB/2025, order dated 1 October 2026
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench
holding_summary: Rujuvalika Investments Limited was, for Tata Steel's purposes, a wholly owned subsidiary holding shares of the parent company, a fairly common structural arrangement inside large corporate groups where an investment vehicle sits between the listed parent and some part of its own shareholding. The scheme sanctioned by the NCLT's Mumbai Bench on 1 October 2026 folds Rujuvalika into Tata Steel, dissolving the subsidiary without a formal winding up and vesting its liabilities directly in the parent. The mechanics of the amalgamation reflect its intra-group, wholly owned character. Tata Steel's own shares that were held by Rujuvalika stand cancelled on the scheme taking effect, and no new shares or cash consideration are issued by Tata Steel in exchange, since there is no outside shareholder in Rujuvalika whose interest needs to be bought out or converted. The appointed date for the scheme, the date from which the merger is treated as effective for accounting purposes, was fixed at the opening of business on 1 April 2023, well over three years before the tribunal's order, underscoring how long these intra-group restructuring exercises can take to work through the statutory process even where there is no third-party opposition. That process itself followed the standard two-motion route under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. The tribunal records that the first motion application was allowed on 25 March 2026, clearing the way for the companies to convene the necessary meetings or seek dispensation from them, followed by a second motion order on 5 June 2026 admitting the scheme for final hearing. The final sanction came roughly four months later.
why_it_matters: Large corporate groups routinely use wholly owned subsidiaries to hold parent-company shares or manage specific asset pools, and periodically need to collapse those subsidiaries back into the parent for simplification or compliance reasons. This sanction confirms the standard sequence, timeline and statutory clearances, Regional Director observations and an Official Liquidator report, that such an uncontested intra-group merger must clear even when there are no minority shareholders or creditors likely to object, giving corporate counsel a current benchmark for planning similar restructurings.
title: NCLT Mumbai Sanctions Tata Steel's Merger With Wholly Owned Subsidiary Rujuvalika Investments
meta_description: NCLT Mumbai approves Tata Steel's amalgamation with its wholly owned subsidiary Rujuvalika Investments, with an appointed date of 1 April 2023.
card_tip: When planning a wholly owned subsidiary merger, budget for the Regional Director's compliance observations and the Official Liquidator's report as routine but necessary steps.

case_name: Kishore Biyani & Rakesh Biyani v. Bank of India & Ors.
citation: Bombay High Court, order dated on or about 3 July 2026, quashing Bank of India's order dated 21 June 2025
holding_summary: Future Lifestyle Fashions Limited's bank account with Bank of India was classified as fraud, and the bank extended that classification to the company's promoters and managing director, including Kishore Biyani and Rakesh Biyani, under the framework the Reserve Bank of India lays down for identifying and reporting fraud in bank accounts. A classification of this kind is not a minor administrative label. Being named in the RBI's Central Fraud Registry carries consequences for future access to credit and banking facilities that follow an individual well beyond the account in question, which is why the procedure leading up to such a classification matters as much as the underlying allegation. Kishore and Rakesh Biyani challenged the classification before the Bombay High Court, and their core complaint was procedural rather than a denial of the underlying facts. Bank of India's order, they argued, did no independent analysis at all. It reproduced portions of a forensic audit report that had examined the accounts, recorded its conclusions, and stopped there, without engaging with the detailed response the petitioners had filed to the bank's show cause notice. A Division Bench of Justices B.P. Colabawalla and Firdosh P. Pooniwalla agreed. It described the bank's order as wholly unreasoned and held that it breached the RBI's 2024 Fraud Master Directions, which require a bank classifying an account as fraud to pass a reasoned order, one that actually grapples with the material the account holder has put forward in response to the show cause notice, rather than simply adopting a third party auditor's findings as its own conclusion without more.
why_it_matters: Fraud classification under the RBI's Master Directions can permanently affect a borrower's or promoter's access to banking facilities through the Central Fraud Registry, making the procedural rigour of the classifying order critically important. This ruling confirms that a bank cannot discharge its obligation to pass a reasoned order simply by reproducing a forensic auditor's conclusions, giving account holders a concrete, high-profile precedent to challenge fraud classifications that fail to engage with their response to the show cause notice.
title: Bombay High Court Quashes Bank of India's Fraud Tag on Kishore and Rakesh Biyani for Lack of Reasons
meta_description: Bombay High Court sets aside Bank of India's fraud tag on the Biyani brothers, holding the order merely reproduced a forensic audit report.
card_tip: When responding to a fraud classification show cause notice, document specific objections to the forensic audit report; an order that fails to engage with those objections is vulnerable to challenge.

case_name: Adani Power (Maharashtra) Limited v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, order dated 19 August 2026, setting aside a Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission order dated 2020
holding_summary: Adani Power's Tiroda thermal plant in Maharashtra has run for years with a change in law compensation mechanism tied to the cost of domestic coal, the kind of arrangement power purchase agreements commonly build in because a generator's fuel cost is not fully within its own control and government policy on coal pricing and allocation shifts periodically after a tariff is set. When a coal shortfall or a change in the applicable coal cost occurs, the generator is entitled to compensation calculated against previously agreed operational parameters, so that neither side bears a cost shock the contract did not allocate to them. The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission had already dealt with the Tiroda plant's domestic coal shortfall compensation issues once, in an order passed in 2020. Adani Power's grievance before APTEL was that MERC, years after that 2020 order, reopened the same settled issues and conducted fresh hearings on questions the Commission had already decided, rather than simply computing the compensation due under the parameters it had itself already fixed. APTEL's bench of Officiating Chairperson Justice Seema Gupta and Technical Member Virender Bhat was unimpressed with that approach. The tribunal pulled up MERC specifically for holding fresh hearings on matters it had treated as settled in 2020, a rebuke aimed at the regulatory process rather than at the substantive compensation formula itself. Reopening a question that has already been decided, without some new and legally sufficient basis for doing so, undermines the finality that a tariff or compensation order is supposed to provide to both the generator and the distribution licensees who have to budget around it.
why_it_matters: Coal-linked change in law compensation disputes between thermal generators and state electricity regulators often drag on for years, with regulators sometimes reopening previously settled computational questions when a generator returns to claim what it is owed. This ruling confirms that APTEL will not tolerate a state commission relitigating parameters it has already fixed in an earlier order, and will impose a firm compliance timeline, giving generators a stronger basis to resist renewed hearings on settled change in law entitlements.
title: APTEL Sets Aside MERC's 2020 Order Capping Domestic Coal Shortfall Compensation for Adani Power's Tiroda Plant
meta_description: APTEL quashes a Maharashtra regulator order that reopened settled coal shortfall compensation issues, directing fresh tariff orders in six weeks.
card_tip: If a state regulator reopens a change in law compensation it already settled, cite this ruling to argue fresh hearings on those parameters are impermissible absent a genuinely new event.

case_name: Central Consumer Protection Authority, Suo Motu Proceedings Against Xboom
citation: Case No. CCPA-2/15/2026-CCPA, order dated 17 September 2026
holding_summary: Xboom had six products listed online under names like X-Mini, X-Radar XK2, X-Eye, X-Gun XK4, RF-Patrol XK2 and XGuard, all of them anti-drone or counter-jamming equipment of the sort normally restricted to defence and security users. None of the listings disclosed that selling or even advertising such equipment requires specific regulatory approvals, a gap that had already drawn the Central Consumer Protection Authority's attention in March 2026 when it flagged Xboom among several e-commerce platforms over unauthorised sale of drone and GPS jammers. A show cause notice followed in February 2026, and the matter was taken to a final order in September. Xboom's defence was that none of this amounted to advertising in the ordinary sense. The company said the six listings existed purely to field enquiries from government and defence buyers, carried no price tags, and offered no way to add anything to a cart, so there was nothing a retail consumer could actually buy off the page. On that reading, a listing without a transaction mechanism falls outside what the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 treats as advertising, and the licensing disclosures the Authority wanted were beside the point. The Authority did not accept that framing. It held that publishing a product listing, complete with specifications and branding, counts as advertising the product regardless of whether a buyer can complete a purchase on that page, and that omitting the licensing requirement from such a listing is a misleading advertisement and an unfair trade practice under the Act. The enquiry-only characterisation did not change what the listing communicated to anyone who saw it, which was that the product was available and said nothing about the approvals needed to possess or import it.
why_it_matters: The CCPA's rejection of Xboom's enquiry-only defence confirms that a product listing counts as an advertisement under the Consumer Protection Act regardless of whether it allows an immediate purchase, closing off a workaround sellers of restricted or licensed goods have used to list products for lead generation without disclosing the regulatory approvals those products actually require before sale or import.
title: CCPA Fines Xboom Rs 10 Lakh, Holds a Product Listing Without a Buy Button Is Still an Advertisement
meta_description: CCPA penalises Xboom for advertising anti-drone and jamming devices without licence disclosures, rejecting its defence that the listings were enquiry-only.
card_tip: Before listing a licence-dependent product online without a purchase option, treat the listing as an advertisement and disclose the applicable approvals on the listing itself.

case_name: Naresh Kumar v. State of U.P. and Another
citation: Allahabad High Court, Criminal Revision, order dated 18 September 2026
holding_summary: Naresh Kumar retired as an Additional District and Sessions Judge, and like every retired judicial officer his pension was revised upward once the Second National Judicial Pay Commission's recommendations came into effect, with arrears paid out on top of the revised monthly figure. When his wife went back to the Family Court seeking an increase in her maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Family Court raised her monthly maintenance from Rs 9,000 to Rs 18,000. Kumar challenged that enhancement in a criminal revision before the Allahabad High Court, and it is there that the pension revision became the central issue. Before the Family Court, Kumar had represented his pension as a fixed figure of Rs 25,632 a month, the amount at which it was originally set. He did not disclose that the pay commission's recommendations had since revised that figure upward, nor did he mention the arrears that followed from the revision. The wife's side pointed to this in the enhancement proceedings, and by the time the matter reached the High Court, Kumar himself did not dispute that he had in fact been receiving close to Rs 88,000 a month after the revision took effect, a figure several times what he had put before the Family Court. Justice Lakshmi Kant Shukla treated that gap as decisive. The judgment records that Kumar had concealed from the Family Court both the pension revision following the pay commission's recommendations and the arrears he received as a result, and finds no legal or jurisdictional error in the Family Court's order that would justify the High Court interfering with it. A litigant seeking to resist or minimise a maintenance obligation cannot do so by presenting an income figure he knows to be outdated while the true, substantially higher figure sits undisclosed.
why_it_matters: The ruling confirms that concealing a pay revision or other income increase in maintenance proceedings exposes a paying spouse to the full consequences of that concealment once discovered, and that remarriage with new dependents is not treated as grounds to cut back a continuing maintenance obligation from an earlier marriage, principles that come up in a large share of Section 125 enhancement disputes.
title: Allahabad HC Doubles Maintenance for Retired Judge's Wife, Says He Hid His Revised Pension
meta_description: Allahabad High Court upholds enhanced maintenance to a retired Additional District Judge's wife after finding he concealed his pay commission arrears.
card_tip: In a maintenance enhancement proceeding, disclose pension, salary or other income revisions fully; concealment discovered later weighs heavily against the paying spouse.

case_name: [Homebuyers] v. Sai Enterprises and Super Construction
citation: MahaRERA, non-compliance/execution application, order dated 8 October 2026 (underlying order dated 31 October 2025)
holding_summary: Two homebuyers had booked a flat through Super Construction in a Thane project then called Sun Gates, later rebranded Sethia Imperial Avenue. In 2018, Super Construction told them that development rights for the project had passed to another entity, Sai Enterprises, and pointed them there instead of handing over what they had paid for. The buyers refused the refund both developers appear to have offered at various points and insisted on the flat itself, a stand that eventually took them before MahaRERA's Member II bench, which on 31 October 2025 directed both developers to allot a specific 795 square foot flat, identified as Flat B07 in Wing B, and to execute a registered agreement for sale within 45 days against payment of any balance consideration still due. That order also fixed what the developers owed on the delay itself. Both were made jointly and severally liable to pay simple interest on Rs 17.49 lakh running from 24 June 2012, the date tied to the buyers' original payments, through to the date possession is actually handed over, and Sai Enterprises was separately directed to pay Rs 20,000 in costs. None of that, the buyers found, translated into compliance. No flat was allotted, no agreement was executed, and the 45 day window closed with nothing done. The buyers returned to MahaRERA with a non-compliance application, which Adjudicating Officer R.K. Malabade decided on 8 October 2026. The developers' response to the non-compliance proceeding reportedly noted that all flats in the project had by then already been sold to third parties, a fact MahaRERA took into account rather than treated as an excuse. Having sold away the very flat it had been ordered to hand over, and the other flats that might have substituted for it, left the developers with nothing to offer in compliance, a position entirely of their own making.
why_it_matters: The order confirms that MahaRERA treats non-compliance with its own allotment or possession directions as an independent wrong attracting a Section 63 penalty, separate from the underlying monetary liability, and that a developer who sells away the disputed unit while an order to allot it is pending gains no relief from that fact; it only forecloses compliance in kind and leaves the penalty and recovery process to run regardless.
title: MahaRERA Fines Two Developers Rs 10 Lakh for Ignoring Its Own Order to Allot a Flat
meta_description: MahaRERA penalises Sai Enterprises and Super Construction Rs 10 lakh for non-compliance with an earlier order to allot a flat and execute an agreement.
card_tip: If a promoter ignores a MahaRERA allotment or possession order, file a non-compliance application to secure a separate Section 63 penalty plus recovery warrants for amounts already due.

case_name: ACC Limited v. State of Karnataka and Others
citation: Karnataka High Court, order dated 8 September 2026
holding_summary: ACC Limited, the Adani Group cement maker, has run a limestone mine at Kalaburagi for years to feed its cement operations, under a mining lease that the state's own mining department treated as having lapsed unless a fresh supplementary lease deed was executed. On that footing, Karnataka's Department of Mines and Geology demanded royalty on a basis ACC disputed, blocked the company's access to the state's ILMS portal used for tracking mineral dispatch, and finally imposed a penalty of Rs 482.69 crore against the company over its Kalaburagi operations. That royalty demand rested on an unusual method. Rather than working from limestone actually extracted, the department calculated what it said ACC owed by applying a notional ratio converting the company's clinker production, the intermediate cement product made from limestone, back into an assumed quantity of limestone consumed. ACC's challenge argued that this notional limestone-to-clinker ratio had no statutory basis and did not reflect what the company had actually mined, and separately that its lease had not lapsed at all because an amendment to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act extended such leases by operation of law. The High Court agreed on both counts. It held that Section 8A(5) of the MMDR Act statutorily extended ACC's mining lease through to 31 March 2030, which meant the lease was in force throughout the period the department had treated as a lapse requiring a fresh deed before operations could continue. Because the lease never lapsed, the department's underlying premise for much of its enforcement action, including the ILMS access block, fell away along with it.
why_it_matters: The ruling confirms that the statutory lease extension under Section 8A(5) of the MMDR Act defeats a state mining department's claim that a lease lapsed for want of a fresh deed, and separately rejects notional clinker-to-limestone conversion as a valid basis for a royalty penalty, giving mineral lease holders facing similar enforcement actions a concrete precedent on both points to rely upon in resisting comparable demands.
title: Karnataka HC Quashes Rs 482 Crore Mining Penalty on ACC, Holds Lease Stood Extended to 2030
meta_description: Karnataka High Court sets aside a Rs 482.69 crore penalty on ACC over its Kalaburagi limestone mine, rejecting the state's clinker-ratio royalty method.
card_tip: If a mining department treats a pre-2015 lease as lapsed for want of a fresh deed, check whether Section 8A(5) of the MMDR Act statutorily extends it before conceding the lapse.

case_name: Kavitha Kuruganti v. PepsiCo India Holdings Private Limited
holding_summary: PepsiCo registered its FL 2027 potato variety, the one grown to feed its Lay's chips line, under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 back in 2016. A few years later the company filed infringement suits against farmers in Gujarat whom it accused of growing FL 2027 without authorisation, a move that provoked a backlash well beyond the individual farmers named, since the suits were widely read as a large multinational using plant breeder's rights to go after small growers. Kavitha Kuruganti, a farmers' rights advocate, responded in 2019 by seeking revocation of PepsiCo's registration itself before the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority. Her revocation application invoked Section 34(h) of the Act, the provision that lets the Authority cancel a registration obtained or exercised in a manner contrary to the public interest. Her case was that filing infringement suits against farmers was itself the kind of public interest violation the section contemplates, since the Act's whole architecture is meant to balance a breeder's commercial rights against farmers' traditional freedom to save, exchange and resow seed. The Authority accepted that argument and revoked PepsiCo's registration in December 2021. PepsiCo took the revocation to the Delhi High Court. A single judge upheld the Authority's revocation in 2023, but a Division Bench reversed that in January 2024 and set the revocation aside, restoring PepsiCo's registration. Both sides then appealed to the Supreme Court, Kuruganti seeking to have the revocation reinstated and PepsiCo defending the Division Bench's restoration of its rights, which is how the matter reached a bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran for what is reported as the first Supreme Court ruling interpreting registration under the 2001 Act.
why_it_matters: The ruling settles, for the first time at the Supreme Court level, that filing infringement suits against farmers does not by itself expose a registered plant variety to revocation under Section 34(h), while confirming that farmers retain an independent, provable defence under Section 39(1)(iv) in any such suit, a balance that will shape how seed companies enforce plant breeder's rights against growers going forward.
title: Supreme Court Upholds PepsiCo's Potato Variety Registration, Leaves Farmers to Prove Their Own Defence
meta_description: Supreme Court holds PepsiCo's FL 2027 potato registration cannot be revoked merely for suing farmers, but sued farmers may still invoke Section 39 rights.
card_tip: A farmer sued for infringing a registered plant variety should plead Section 39(1)(iv) of the PPV&FR Act as a specific, provable defence, not assume the registration's validity decides the case.

case_name: Tata Capital Financial Services Limited (now Tata Capital Limited) v. Neel Motors LLP and Others
citation: Commercial Arbitration Petition No. 620 of 2021
holding_summary: Tata Capital Financial Services, now merged into Tata Capital Limited, had extended credit to Neel Motors LLP under a Channel Finance Agreement, with four individuals standing as personal guarantors. When the loan soured, Tata Capital moved a Commercial Arbitration Petition, numbered 620 of 2021, seeking to proceed against the guarantors. The guarantors resisted on a familiar ground in recent personal insolvency litigation, pointing to Section 95 applications they had filed before the NCLT, which under the unamended Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code triggered an interim moratorium shielding a personal guarantor from exactly this kind of proceeding the moment such an application is filed. That shield changed shape in 2026. Parliament amended Sections 96 and 124 of the Code to insert a new sub-section excluding personal guarantors of corporate debtors from the interim moratorium altogether, with the change taking effect from 26 May 2026. The practical question before Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan was not whether the amendment existed, both sides agreed it did, but whether it reached insolvency applications the guarantors had filed before that date, applications that were already pending when the new sub-section came into force. The guarantors argued for a narrow reading confined to future filings. Their position was that the amendment should only apply to Section 95 applications filed on or after 26 May 2026, leaving their own pending applications, filed earlier, governed by the old regime and its interim moratorium. On that reading, Tata Capital's arbitration against them would remain stayed notwithstanding the amendment, simply because the guarantors had gotten their applications in before the cut-off date.
why_it_matters: The ruling closes off a tactic some personal guarantors used, filing a Section 95 insolvency application to trigger an interim moratorium and stall a lender's arbitration or recovery proceedings, by confirming that the 2026 amendment removing that moratorium for guarantors of corporate debtors applies equally to applications already pending on its effective date, besides fresh filings made afterward, a reading the IBBI has since echoed in its own circular.
title: Bombay HC Holds New IBC Rule Stripping Guarantors of Interim Moratorium Applies to Pending Cases Too
meta_description: Bombay High Court lets Tata Capital pursue arbitration against personal guarantors, holding the 2026 IBC amendment covers insolvency pleas filed earlier.
card_tip: Before relying on a guarantor's pending Section 95 insolvency application to resist recovery, check whether the 2026 amendment to Sections 96 and 124 of the IBC has already removed that protection.

case_name: State Bank of India v. Garden Court Distilleries Private Limited and Another
citation: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1138 and 1145 of 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: Garden Court Distilleries Private Limited went into liquidation on 10 October 2025, when the NCLT's Ahmedabad Bench admitted the company under Section 33(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. That order itself recorded that the committee of creditors had already decided to first explore selling the company as a going concern rather than breaking it up for piecemeal asset sales, the preferred route under the liquidation regulations wherever a buyer for the whole business can realistically be found. Four days after the liquidation order, on 14 October 2025, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India amended Regulation 39C of the liquidation process regulations, the provision bearing on how a going-concern sale is to be conducted. When a successful bidder later approached the NCLT seeking reliefs to actually implement the going-concern sale that had by then been identified, the NCLT, in an order dated 17 June 2026, applied the amended version of Regulation 39C and rejected the bidder's application on that basis, treating the later amendment as governing the sale process even though the liquidation itself had commenced before the amendment existed. The bidder and the financial creditor, State Bank of India, carried that rejection up to the NCLAT in two connected appeals. Their argument was that a going-concern liquidation sale is not a free-standing event separate from the liquidation order that set it in motion, it is simply the mode of liquidation the committee had already chosen inside that order, so the regulations governing the sale had to be the regulations in force on 10 October 2025, the date the liquidation order itself was passed, not whatever version of Regulation 39C happened to exist by the time implementation reliefs came up for decision months later.
why_it_matters: The ruling fixes that the regulatory framework governing a going-concern liquidation sale is locked in on the date the Section 33 liquidation order is passed, not on the date a subsequent IBBI amendment happens to take effect, giving liquidators, bidders and creditors a clear basis to resist an adjudicating authority applying a later amendment to a sale process already under way, and pressing for a quick remand decision where delay threatens the business's ongoing viability.
title: NCLAT: Going-Concern Sale Is Governed by Rules on the Liquidation Order Date, Not a Later Amendment
meta_description: NCLAT sets aside an NCLT order that applied a later IBBI regulation amendment to a going-concern sale, remanding Garden Court Distilleries' liquidation.
card_tip: In a going-concern liquidation sale, fix the applicable IBBI regulations by the date of the Section 33 liquidation order itself, not the date a sale implementation application is finally decided.

case_name: High Point Supply Company LLC v. Agati Healthcare Private Limited
citation: Commercial First Appeal No. 15 of 2026 (COMFA/15/2026)
holding_summary: High Point Supply Company, a US distributor, held exclusive rights to sell a colostrum based nutrition product across North America, sourced from Agati Healthcare, a Navi Mumbai manufacturer, under a distribution agreement running through June 2026. The arrangement came under strain after the brand on the product's US side was acquired by Glanbia Nutritionals. High Point's case was that Agati then started supplying the same product directly to Glanbia, bypassing High Point's exclusivity, before terminating the distribution agreement itself. The distributor sued Agati in the trial court seeking an injunction against the continuing breach along with consequential monetary relief, and asked for urgent interim protection without first going through the pre-institution mediation that Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act otherwise makes mandatory for commercial suits. Section 12A carries a built-in exception for suits that contemplate urgent interim relief, letting a plaintiff skip mediation and go straight to court where genuine urgency exists, and High Point's suit was framed to fall within that exception. That characterisation failed at the trial court stage. The judge rejected the plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, reasoning that High Point's claim was really for quantifiable monetary damages dressed up with an injunction, and separately noting that High Point had not moved with the urgency its own pleadings claimed, since some time had passed between Agati's termination notice and the suit being filed. On that combined reasoning, the suit was held non-maintainable for want of prior mediation.
why_it_matters: The ruling draws a clear line between the limited jurisdictional inquiry a court must make when testing the Section 12A urgent relief exception to pre-institution mediation and the fuller merits based triple test applied at the interim injunction stage, preventing trial courts from using Order VII Rule 11 to dispose of commercial suits on a premature assessment of whether relief will be granted.
title: Bombay HC Restores Distributor's Suit, Says Courts Can't Weigh Merits When Testing the Urgent Relief Exception
meta_description: Bombay High Court revives a US distributor's suit against Agati Healthcare, holding the Section 12A urgency exception needs only a limited threshold check.
card_tip: When pleading the Section 12A urgent relief exception to mediation, frame the continuing breach clearly on the plaint's face; delay alone should not disqualify it at this threshold stage.

case_name: In Re: Flipkart Internet Private Limited (Cyclosinone Herbicide proceedings)
citation: Central Consumer Protection Authority, order dated 22 September 2026
holding_summary: A weed killer sold online as a 'Farmer and Gardener Approved Weed Killer' has cost Flipkart a Rs 10 lakh penalty, after the Central Consumer Protection Authority found that the chemical behind the label, Cyclosinone, does not exist in the Schedule to the Insecticides Act, 1968 at all. The Crop Care Federation of India had written to the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare on 22 January 2026 flagging the listings, and the Department forwarded the complaint to the CCPA on 18 February 2026. By September the Authority had traced the same product across three marketplaces and penalised each of them separately. The Authority's order against Flipkart Internet Private Limited records that the platform had listed, advertised and facilitated sale of Cyclosinone Herbicide to buyers who had no way of knowing that no insecticide or herbicide by that name is registered anywhere under Indian law. An unregistered agro-chemical is not a labelling technicality. The Insecticides Act exists precisely to keep untested chemical formulations away from crops and the people who eat what those crops produce, and a product that has never cleared that registration process carries no assurance about what it actually contains or does to soil, produce or the farmer handling it. Flipkart's defence followed a pattern familiar to anyone who has watched e-commerce platforms answer for third-party listings: it said it was merely an intermediary, that the seller had uploaded the product and its claims, and that responsibility for an unregistered chemical being sold under a false approval claim belonged to that seller and not to the marketplace carrying the listing. The Authority was not persuaded. It held that Flipkart's own role in listing, advertising and facilitating the sale carried statutory due diligence obligations under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, obligations that do not evaporate merely because the seller, not the platform, physically fulfilled the order.
why_it_matters: The order confirms that an e-commerce marketplace cannot treat a seller's product claims as someone else's problem once a trade body complains; the CCPA will treat listing and advertising an unregistered agro-chemical as the platform's own unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, exposing marketplaces to direct penalties for third-party agricultural product claims they never independently verified before publishing them to buyers.
title: CCPA Fines Flipkart Rs 10 Lakh for Listing an Unregistered 'Cyclosinone' Herbicide, Rejects Marketplace Defence
meta_description: CCPA fines Flipkart, Amazon and JioMart over an unregistered agro-chemical weed killer, holding a marketplace cannot hide behind its seller's claims.
card_tip: Marketplaces carrying agro-chemical listings should verify registration under the Insecticides Act before a product goes live, not after a trade body complains.

case_name: Mahinder and Others v. Puran Singh
holding_summary: A dispute over farmland in Karnal, Haryana, has given the Supreme Court occasion to settle a question several High Courts had answered differently for years: does the preferential right of purchase given to co-heirs under Section 22 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 apply to agricultural land, or only to other kinds of inherited property. A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and N. Kotiswar Singh has now held, in Mahinder and Others v. Puran Singh, that it does. The facts were straightforward. Co-heirs had inherited land in Karnal, and one of them sold his undivided share to an outsider without first offering it to the other Class I heirs, who then sued to exercise their statutory right to step into the buyer's shoes on the same terms. The trial court and the First Appellate Court both ruled for the co-heirs, as did the High Court, and the outsider carried the matter to the Supreme Court arguing that a provision of this kind, which restricts an owner's freedom to sell to whomever he pleases, could not survive constitutional scrutiny when applied to agricultural land, a category long treated as a sensitive subject for legislative competence. That argument rested heavily on Atam Prakash v. State of Haryana, the 1986 Constitution Bench ruling that struck down a provision of the Punjab Pre-emption Act granting a right of pre-emption to certain classes of relatives over agricultural land, on the ground that it was an anachronistic restraint on alienation with no rational basis in a modern property regime. If pre-emption rights over farmland could not survive under one statute, the appellant argued, Section 22 should meet the same fate when it operates on farmland too.
why_it_matters: Buyers of undivided shares in inherited agricultural land, and the co-heirs they buy from, now face a settled Supreme Court position that the other co-heirs can step in and buy out that share on the same terms, closing off a defence that farmland sits outside Section 22's reach and giving family members a clearer route to keep jointly inherited land within the family rather than litigating the threshold applicability question afresh in every state.
title: Supreme Court Holds Section 22 Pre-Emption Right Under Hindu Succession Act Extends to Agricultural Land
meta_description: SC settles a long split among High Courts, ruling that a co-heir's right to buy out a stranger's share under Section 22 HSA applies to farmland too.
card_tip: Before buying an undivided share of inherited agricultural land from one co-heir, check whether the other Class I heirs have been given notice of their Section 22 pre-emption right.

case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. The Louis Berger Group Inc. (JV with COWI A/S)
citation: O.M.P. (COMM) 351/2023, decided 3 August 2026
holding_summary: A consultancy dispute tracing back to a bridge collapse in 2009 has produced a fresh ruling on how far an arbitral tribunal can go in compensating a contractor for work it has not yet performed. The National Highways Authority of India had engaged The Louis Berger Group, in joint venture with COWI A/S, for design, construction supervision and operation and maintenance of a cable-stayed bridge across the Chambal river at Kota, Rajasthan. The partly built structure collapsed in December 2009, and NHAI kept the consultant engaged through the aftermath, which eventually produced a dispute over unpaid fees and O&M charges that went to arbitration. The tribunal awarded the consultant roughly Rs 5.16 crore and USD 60,769 with interest, a sum that included not just amounts already due but a component for future operation and maintenance services the consultant had not yet rendered by the date of the award. NHAI challenged the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the Delhi High Court has now set aside that future O&M component while leaving the rest of the award standing. Justice Avneesh Jhingan's reasoning turned on a point that recurs often enough in long-running infrastructure contracts to matter well beyond this one bridge: relief cannot be granted for an apprehended future liability when no amount was actually due on the date the award was made. The consultant had argued it would go on providing O&M services and should be paid for that continuing obligation up front, but the Court held that awarding money for services yet to be rendered, where no sum had crystallised as owed, goes beyond the scope of what the parties submitted to arbitration and falls within the specific ground for setting aside an award under Section 34(2)(a)(iv) of the Act.
why_it_matters: Public infrastructure authorities facing arbitral awards that bundle future service payments with accrued dues now have a clear basis to isolate and challenge only the forward-looking component, while contractors drafting claims against NHAI and similar authorities should limit relief sought to amounts already due rather than a lump-sum valuation of continuing obligations that a reviewing court is likely to sever out under Section 34.
title: Delhi HC Partly Sets Aside NHAI Arbitral Award, Holds Future O&M Claims Fell Outside Arbitration's Scope
meta_description: Delhi High Court severs a consultant's future operation and maintenance claim from an award on the Chambal cable-stayed bridge, upholding the rest.
card_tip: When seeking relief in arbitration against a public authority for a continuing service contract, confine the claim to amounts already due rather than a forward valuation of future performance.

case_name: Manas Shelters Private Limited v. Vivek Madhavlal Pittie
citation: Interim Application No. 4450 of 2026 in Commercial Suit No. 344 of 2015, order dated 2 September 2026
holding_summary: A redevelopment dispute over a Tardeo property that has already travelled through a Single Judge, a Division Bench and the Supreme Court is still not close to a final decision on its merits, after the Bombay High Court refused to decide it on summary judgment and sent it instead for a full trial. Manas Shelters Private Limited had sued Vivek Madhavlal Pittie over the development arrangement for C.S. No. 321, Tardeo Division, Pathe Baburao Marg, Mumbai, after the original owner terminated the arrangement on 16 July 2013, alleging that Manas had failed to perform its contractual obligations. Manas did not accept that termination and fought it for over a decade on more than one front before this suit reached the stage at which it is now. It first obtained interim protection restraining the owner from dealing with the property, protection that the Single Judge eventually vacated on 27 March 2024. A Division Bench dismissed Manas's appeal against that vacation on 24 June 2025, and the Supreme Court dismissed its special leave petition on 19 February 2026, closing off every avenue by which Manas could keep the interim injunction alive. With the injunction gone, Manas turned to the underlying suit itself and sought summary judgment and judgment on admissions, asking the Court to declare the 2013 termination illegal outright and to decree in its favour Rs 31,10,00,449 with interest, without putting the dispute through a trial. Summary judgment under Order XIII-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, as applicable to commercial suits, is available only where the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim, a fairly high threshold meant to weed out suits where a trial would serve no purpose.
why_it_matters: Commercial litigants seeking summary judgment under Order XIII-A in high-value redevelopment and contract disputes should expect a court to insist on full trial wherever quantum, causation or readiness to perform remain genuinely contested, and a weak track record at the interim injunction stage will count against a later summary judgment application even though the two proceedings test formally different questions.
title: Bombay HC Refuses Summary Judgment in Rs 31 Crore Tardeo Redevelopment Suit, Orders Full Trial
meta_description: Bombay HC declines a developer's summary judgment bid, holding termination, readiness and a Rs 31.10 crore damages claim need trial and evidence.
card_tip: Before applying for summary judgment on a large damages claim, assess whether questions of readiness to perform, causation and quantum can genuinely be resolved without oral evidence.

case_name: Dharmendra Hansraj Kotak & Ors. v. State of Delhi & Anr.
citation: Delhi High Court, Section 482 CrPC petition, order dated 6 August 2026
holding_summary: Eleven years after Food Safety Officers in Delhi pulled packets of Maggi noodles off retail shelves for testing, the criminal case built on those samples has finally come to an end. The Delhi High Court has quashed the complaints, the summoning orders issued in 2015 and 2016, and all proceedings that followed against Nestle India's distributors and other persons connected with the manufacture and sale of the product, holding that making them stand trial any longer would amount to an abuse of the process of the court. The prosecution traced back to May 2015, when Food Safety Officers collected Maggi samples in Delhi as part of the nationwide scare that followed similar findings in other states. The Food Analyst's reports said the lead content in the masala tastemaker sachet exceeded the permissible limit of 2.5 parts per million under food safety regulations, and a separate complaint alleged misbranding over the product's 'No Added MSG' label. On the strength of those reports, criminal complaints were filed and summoning orders issued against the petitioners, who approached the High Court years later under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, invoking the Court's inherent power to prevent the misuse of the criminal process. What changed the picture, and what the Court treated as decisive, was what happened to the scientific foundation of the original Food Analyst reports in the intervening years. The Supreme Court, hearing the broader Maggi litigation, had directed fresh testing of the product by CSIR-Central Food Technological Research Institute in Mysore under its own supervision, a step meant to settle the underlying safety question independently of the original state-level sampling. Those CFTRI reports found the relevant parameters, including lead content, within permissible limits, directly at odds with what the original Delhi samples had shown.
why_it_matters: Food business operators facing a prosecution built on a single adverse laboratory report now have a concrete precedent for using a later, court-supervised referral test with a contrary finding to seek quashing under Section 482 rather than waiting out a full trial, while regulators are reminded that a prosecution's scientific foundation can be overtaken by subsequent testing ordered in connected proceedings years after the original complaint was filed.
title: Delhi HC Quashes 11-Year-Old Maggi Lead Prosecution, Says Fresh CFTRI Tests Eroded the Case
meta_description: Delhi High Court ends the 2015 Maggi lead prosecution against Nestle distributors, holding continued proceedings would abuse the process of court.
card_tip: If a court-supervised referral test later contradicts the Food Analyst report underlying a pending prosecution, consider a Section 482 CrPC petition rather than contesting only at trial.

case_name: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
holding_summary: A truck owner who watched his vehicle driven away in the middle of the night by men he did not know, only to discover later that they had been sent by his own financier, has produced a Supreme Court ruling that goes well beyond his individual case to question whether the Reserve Bank of India's recovery guidelines mean anything in practice at all. Hari Dutta Sharma had taken a commercial vehicle loan from Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company in 2019, secured by hypothecation of the truck, and the financier had already repossessed and released the vehicle once before, in 2022, after an earlier default. In April 2023 the truck was taken again, this time at night and without the seven-day notice the loan agreement itself required before any repossession. Sharma's writ petition before the Allahabad High Court was dismissed, reportedly on grounds of delay in approaching the court, leaving him to carry the matter to the Supreme Court. A bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe allowed his appeal, finding that the manner of repossession, not merely the underlying default, was itself unlawful. The Court held that a night-time seizure of a hypothecated vehicle, carried out without the contractual notice period the financier's own loan agreement promised the borrower, violates Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. A financier's right to recover security on default does not translate into a licence to use force or surprise against the borrower; the contractual right to repossess, the Court held, can only be exercised through the safeguards the agreement itself, and the RBI's fair practices guidelines, build around that right, not by sending agents to take the vehicle in the dark before the borrower has had the notice period he bargained for.
why_it_matters: NBFCs and banks can no longer treat repossession of hypothecated vehicles as a purely contractual or operational matter to be executed by recovery agents at their convenience; a seizure that skips the agreed notice period or occurs through force or at night now exposes the lender to a constitutional challenge and compensation, and the RBI faces a direct Supreme Court mandate to make its recovery guidelines actually enforceable rather than advisory.
title: Supreme Court Holds Night-Time Vehicle Repossession Without Notice Violates Articles 14 and 21
meta_description: SC rules a financier cannot repossess a hypothecated vehicle by force or at night without the contractual notice, and directs RBI to enforce compliance.
card_tip: Before authorising a vehicle repossession, confirm the contractual notice period has run and that no agent will act by force or outside daylight hours.

case_name: Parshvadhara Complex ABCD Co-operative Housing Society v. M/s. Parshwanath Developers & Ors.
citation: Appeal No. AT006000000345557 of 2024, MahaREAT, arising from Complaint No. CC006000000020890 of 2022 before the MahaRERA Authority
holding_summary: The Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal has told a Thane developer that a planning sanction obtained years after flats were sold cannot stand in for the buyers' own consent to a fresh building on the same plot. By an order dated 7 September 2026, the tribunal dismissed the promoter's appeal and partly allowed a cross-appeal filed by the project's housing society, in a dispute over an entire additional wing raised at the Parshvadhara project at Belavali in Ambernath taluka, Thane district. Buyers at Parshvadhara booked their flats against a layout that did not show what later became Wing E. The promoter, M/s. Parshwanath Developers, obtained a revised sanction on 2 July 2021 permitting an additional building on the same plot, and went ahead and built it. The housing society, formed by the allottees once their flats were handed over, took the position that nobody who had already paid for a flat on the strength of the original layout had agreed to a new wing coming up alongside their homes, and that a later municipal approval did not change that. The society first raised the grievance before the MahaRERA Authority, in Complaint No. CC006000000020890 of 2022. On 30 August 2024, the Authority held that the promoter needed the consent of two-thirds of the allottees before proceeding with the additional wing, and restrained further construction until that consent was secured. Both sides were dissatisfied. The promoter appealed, pointing to the revised sanction as its answer to the consent requirement. The society cross-appealed, arguing the Authority ought to have ordered the already-built wing removed rather than merely pausing further work on a structure that, by then, largely stood complete.
why_it_matters: Developers routinely treat a later-obtained statutory sanction as sufficient cover for additional construction on an already-sold project. This order holds that such a sanction answers only the planning-law question, not the separate requirement under MOFA and RERA that allottees give specific, informed consent to that particular construction. Housing societies facing unauthorised additions elsewhere in Maharashtra now have appellate authority for seeking demolition, not merely a freeze on further work, plus penalty and conveyance relief in the same proceeding.
title: MahaREAT Orders Demolition of Unauthorised Wing Built Without Allottees' Consent in Thane Project
meta_description: Maharashtra's real estate appellate tribunal holds a later building sanction cannot replace allottees' specific consent, and orders a wing demolished.
card_tip: A statutory building sanction obtained after flats are sold does not satisfy RERA's consent requirement; promoters need specific, informed allottee consent for each additional structure.

case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. Bareilly Highways Project Limited
citation: Arbitral award disclosed via official NHAI statement issued 27 July 2026; exact date of signing of the award not disclosed in public reporting
court: Arbitral Tribunal (ad hoc, constituted under the concession agreement)
holding_summary: A concessionaire that terminated its concession agreement with the National Highways Authority of India in 2019 and went after it for over three thousand crore rupees has come away with less than two per cent of what it asked for. An Arbitral Tribunal has allowed only three of the thirty claims raised by Bareilly Highways Project Limited, totalling about Rs 46 crore plus applicable interest, against a demand of roughly Rs 3,177 crore, in an award disclosed through an official NHAI statement issued on 27 July 2026. The dispute goes back to the Bareilly-Sitapur BOT toll project in Uttar Pradesh, a 151-kilometre highway stretch that NHAI terminated in May 2019. The concessionaire behind the project, Bareilly Highways Project Limited, is a company promoted by Era Infra Engineering. Once the concession ended, BHPL took the dispute to arbitration, raising thirty separate claims that together ran into the thousands of crores, covering losses it said it suffered over the life of the project and on termination. Central to the Tribunal's reasoning was a Supplementary Agreement dated 30 March 2015, which it treated as governing the parties' rights and obligations for the period in dispute. Working from that agreement, the Tribunal concluded that the delays which plagued the project were concurrent, meaning both NHAI and the concessionaire bore responsibility for the slippages, rather than the fault lying with NHAI alone as BHPL's claims assumed. That single finding did most of the work in the award. Once the delays were treated as shared rather than attributable to NHAI, the bulk of BHPL's claims for losses flowing from those delays had no basis to stand on.
why_it_matters: NHAI faces a steady stream of multi-thousand-crore arbitration claims from concessionaires whose BOT contracts were terminated, and how tribunals treat delay attribution decides most of these cases. A concurrent-delay finding, as here, can reduce a claim by well over ninety per cent regardless of its headline size. Concessionaires preparing termination claims, and the authority defending them, both need to reckon with how much weight a tribunal is likely to put on shared responsibility for project delays before litigating the quantum.
title: Arbitral Tribunal Cuts Rs 3,177 Crore Claim Against NHAI to Rs 46 Crore Over Bareilly-Sitapur Toll Road
meta_description: A tribunal allows only three of thirty claims by the Bareilly-Sitapur BOT concessionaire, finding the project delays were concurrent, not NHAI's alone.
card_tip: In BOT termination arbitrations, a concurrent-delay finding can wipe out the bulk of a concessionaire's claim regardless of its headline value; delay attribution usually decides the quantum.

case_name: Petitioner (husband) & Anr. v. State of Kerala & Anr. (parties not named in available reporting)
citation: 2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 512; Crl.M.C. No. 5128 of 2026
holding_summary: A husband and his mother asked the Kerala High Court to shut down a domestic violence complaint on the ground that the wife had waited years before approaching a magistrate. Justice Jobin Sebastian turned them down on 10 September 2026, holding that the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act sets no deadline for filing such a complaint, and that delay by itself is not a ground to quash proceedings already pending before a trial court. The wife had filed her complaint under Section 12 of the Act before the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-III, Thrissur, registered as M.C. No. 32/2025. The husband and mother-in-law moved the High Court under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the provision that now carries the quashing jurisdiction once exercised under Section 482 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure, seeking to have the proceedings thrown out at the threshold. Their case rested on two limbs. First, they said the wife had let roughly six years pass after the parties separated before lodging her complaint, and that such a long, unexplained gap should be fatal to the proceedings. Second, they argued the complaint was retaliatory, pointing out that it came only after the husband had moved the Family Court for compensation in connection with an earlier POCSO case. The wife disputed the delay figure and pointed to a specific allegation of violence as recent as May 2025, which she said the petitioners' framing of the timeline ignored.
why_it_matters: Petitioners facing domestic violence complaints filed long after a marital separation routinely argue that delay alone should end the case at the threshold. This ruling closes that route in Kerala by confirming the PWDV Act fixes no limitation period for a Section 12 complaint, and that both delay and claims of retaliatory motive are matters for trial on evidence, not grounds for quashing under the High Court's inherent jurisdiction. Family law practitioners advising either side need to plan around a full hearing rather than an early exit.
title: Kerala High Court: Delay Alone in Filing a Domestic Violence Complaint Does Not Justify Quashing It
meta_description: Justice Jobin Sebastian holds the PWDV Act sets no limitation period for a Section 12 complaint, and refuses to quash over a husband's delay plea.
card_tip: A long gap before filing a Section 12 PWDV Act complaint is not by itself a ground for quashing; courts treat delay and claims of retaliatory motive as questions for trial, not threshold dismissal.

case_name: HDFC Bank Ltd. v. Kishore K. Mehta (Dead) Thr. LRs
holding_summary: A bank holding a recovery certificate from the Debts Recovery Tribunal has long treated it as good as a decree, something it can use to chase a defaulting borrower through whatever forum promises the fastest result. The Supreme Court has now told HDFC Bank that a recovery certificate issued before November 2016 does not carry that weight for one particular purpose: triggering an insolvency notice against an individual under the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act, 1909. The dispute traced back to 2004. The Debts Recovery Tribunal directed issuance of a recovery certificate against Kishore K. Mehta for a little over Rs 14.74 crore on 26 October that year, and the certificate itself followed on 30 November 2004. Years later, the bank sought to use that certificate as the foundation for a Section 9(2) insolvency notice against Mehta, arguing that a recovery certificate was the functional equivalent of a decree or order of a court, the kind of instrument the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act accepts as the basis for such a notice. Mehta's representatives challenged the notice before the Bombay High Court. A single judge quashed it, a Division Bench affirmed that view, and the bank carried the fight to the Supreme Court. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma were unpersuaded by the bank's position and dismissed the appeal.
why_it_matters: Banks and NBFCs holding old, pre-2016 DRT recovery certificates against individual guarantors or borrowers cannot treat those certificates as decrees for the purpose of launching insolvency notices under the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act. Lenders pursuing legacy recovery files from the early 2000s need to fall back on ordinary DRT execution, not personal insolvency proceedings, unless their recovery certificate post-dates the 2016 amendment to Section 19 of the RDB Act.
title: Pre-2016 DRT Recovery Certificates Cannot Found an Insolvency Notice, Holds Supreme Court
meta_description: Supreme Court rules a DRT recovery certificate issued before the 2016 RDB Act amendment cannot support a Section 9(2) insolvency notice against a borrower.
card_tip: Check the date of any recovery certificate before relying on it for an insolvency notice: only certificates issued after the 2016 RDB Act amendment carry decree-like status for that purpose.

case_name: All India Trade Union Congress & Others v. State of Karnataka & Others
citation: Writ petitions filed by AITUC and others, Karnataka High Court, interim order dated 18-19 September 2026, staying circulars dated 29 July, 10 August and 28 August 2026
holding_summary: Three trade unions have managed to stop the Karnataka government's own departments from sitting on a wage hike the government itself announced. The Karnataka High Court has stayed a set of circulars that told local bodies and audit departments to hold back a revised minimum wage notification, in a dispute that pits the state's left hand against its right. The State notified revised minimum wage rates for 81 scheduled employments on 22 May 2026. Rather than roll out the hike, three arms of the government, the Karnataka State Audit and Accounts Department, the Directorate of Municipal Administration, and the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department, issued circulars on 29 July, 10 August and 28 August directing local authorities to defer or suspend implementation for outsourced and contract staff. No court had stayed the May notification at that point, and none has since. Three unions, the All India Trade Union Congress, the Karnataka Rajya Sarkari Khayametharara Noukarara Okkuta and the All India Central Council of Trade Unions, moved the High Court against these circulars. Their case was straightforward: a statutory wage notification cannot be suspended by executive circular, and departments lacked any legal authority to override a notification that stood unchallenged and unstayed. Justice H.T. Narendra Prasad accepted that logic for the purposes of interim relief and stayed the circulars, leaving the May notification operative while the matter proceeds to full hearing.
why_it_matters: Government departments cannot use internal circulars to defer or suspend a statutory minimum wage notification that has not been stayed by any court. Employers, both private and public-body contractors in Karnataka, must now pay the revised May 2026 rates to outsourced and contract staff while the deeper question, whether the 2019 Code on Wages has overridden the 1948 Act, awaits a Division Bench ruling in connected appeals.
title: Karnataka High Court Stays Circulars That Deferred Revised Minimum Wages for Contract Workers
meta_description: Karnataka HC stays circulars deferring the May 2026 minimum wage hike for contract staff; a separate employers' challenge awaits a Division Bench.
card_tip: A circular cannot override an unstayed statutory wage notification; apply the revised Karnataka minimum wage rates unless a court has specifically stayed the notification itself.

case_name: Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited & Anr. v. Regional Director, Southeastern Region & Anr.
citation: Company Appeal (AT)(CH) No. 88 of 2026, NCLAT Chennai Bench, order dated 25 September 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench
holding_summary: A tribunal asked only to let shareholders and creditors vote on a merger ended up deciding the merger was flawed before anyone got to vote at all. The NCLAT's Chennai Bench has corrected that sequence, reviving the proposed merger of Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited into GOCL Corporation Limited after the NCLT's Amravati Bench had thrown out the scheme at the earliest possible stage. The timeline mattered to how the appeal turned out. SEBI's observation report on the scheme came in on 20 May 2026, with BSE's observation letter arriving the same day and NSE's two days later. HNPCL and GOCL filed their first motion application before the NCLT on 22 June, roughly a month after clearing the exchange and regulatory observations. The NCLT nonetheless rejected the application on 30 July, on two grounds: that the scheme's appointed date was more than a year before the filing date without adequate justification under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' General Circular 09/2019, and that the companies' financials showed unexplained discrepancies. On appeal, the companies argued that both objections were raised too soon and rested on an incomplete picture. The delay between the appointed date and the filing, they said, was explained precisely by the time taken waiting for SEBI, BSE and NSE to clear the scheme, a wait that was neither the companies' fault nor unusual for a listed-company merger of this size. The NCLAT agreed, finding it unfair to penalise the companies for a regulatory timeline that was largely out of their hands.
why_it_matters: Companies pursuing a merger or demerger scheme can cite this ruling to resist a tribunal rejecting the proposal at the first motion stage over an appointed date that predates filing because of time spent awaiting SEBI, BSE or NSE observations, or over financial discrepancies that have not yet been tested at a sanction hearing. The ruling confirms that threshold-stage scrutiny under Sections 230-232 is limited, and that commercial questions about a scheme belong to shareholders and creditors first, and to objectors only at the later sanction stage.
title: NCLAT Says Tribunal Jumped the Gun in Rejecting HNPCL-GOCL Merger at First Motion Stage
meta_description: NCLAT sets aside NCLT's rejection of the HNPCL-GOCL merger, holding scrutiny on appointed date and financials was premature before shareholder meetings.
card_tip: If a tribunal rejects a merger at first motion over a long appointed-date gap, check whether that gap tracks time spent awaiting SEBI or exchange observations.

case_name: D v. S
citation: 2026 INSC 1043, decided 23 September 2026
holding_summary: A custody fight that had already run more than seven years, through a Family Court, the Delhi High Court, and now the Supreme Court, has ended with the mother cleared to take her two children to the United Kingdom, where she works as a university lecturer, while the father is left without custody for as long as a pending POCSO case against him remains unresolved. The Family Court had given the father sole custody back in 2024, and the Delhi High Court affirmed that order in January 2026. Both courts had to grapple with a POCSO prosecution pending against the father, and both had, in different ways, commented on how credible they found the allegations behind that FIR. The Supreme Court took issue with exactly that part of the reasoning when the mother appealed. Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta laid down a clean rule for cases like this one: a parent facing a pending prosecution under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act cannot be treated as entitled to custody, whatever the eventual outcome of that criminal case turns out to be, for as long as the prosecution remains alive. Courts hearing a custody dispute are not the forum to pre-judge a POCSO trial, and they should not lean on their own view of the FIR's merits to decide who gets the child.
why_it_matters: Family courts and High Courts deciding custody while a parent faces a pending POCSO case can no longer use their own assessment of the FIR's credibility to decide the dispute; that question belongs to the criminal trial court alone. The ruling also warns against treating a parent's career-driven relocation or job changes as proof of parental unsuitability, a point relevant well beyond POCSO-linked custody disputes to any case where one parent's mobility is used against them.
title: A Parent Facing Pending POCSO Prosecution Cannot Get Custody, Rules Supreme Court While Allowing Relocation to UK
meta_description: Supreme Court lets a mother relocate her children to the UK and denies the father custody while his POCSO case is pending, expunging the HC's remarks.
card_tip: In a custody case involving a pending POCSO prosecution, do not ask the family court to assess the FIR's merits; custody can be withheld on the bare fact of the pending case.

case_name: Hotel Alankar v. State of Maharashtra
citation: 2026 BHC KOL 8650 (DB)
holding_summary: An establishment that fixes the problems a food safety inspector flagged should get its licence back, not keep answering for a violation that no longer exists. That, in essence, is what the Bombay High Court's Kolhapur Bench told the State of Maharashtra when a food business authority tried to keep a suspension running well after the hotel it targeted had cleaned up its act. The sequence of inspections told its own story. A surprise inspection on 7 July 2026 found the hotel's food safety compliance at just 69 per cent, and the licensing authority suspended its licence the very next day under Section 32(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, the provision that lets an authority act immediately where public health is at stake. The hotel moved quickly to fix what the inspection had found, and a re-inspection on 31 July recorded 97 per cent compliance, a figure the Division Bench treated as proof that the underlying public health concern had been resolved. Despite that turnaround, the suspension was kept in place, prompting the hotel to approach the High Court. Justices Sharmila U. Deshmukh and Neeraj P. Dhote framed the question squarely: does Section 32(3) authorise an open-ended suspension, or is it confined to the period during which the public health risk that justified it actually persists? The bench came down firmly on the latter reading.
why_it_matters: Food businesses facing a Section 32(3) FSSAI licence suspension now have High Court authority for the proposition that a strong re-inspection score should end the suspension, shifting the burden onto the licensing authority to identify any specific, ongoing public health risk if it wants to keep the suspension alive. The ruling does not shield an establishment from separate penalties for the original lapse or for operating in breach of a validly imposed suspension, but it stops authorities from treating suspension itself as an indefinite punishment.
title: FSSAI Licence Suspension Cannot Continue Once Compliance Is Restored, Rules Bombay High Court
meta_description: Bombay HC's Kolhapur Bench holds an FSSAI licence suspension must be revoked once re-inspection shows compliance, rejecting its use as a standing penalty.
card_tip: After a Section 32(3) suspension, get a prompt re-inspection and use a strong score to press for revocation; absent a specific, ongoing risk, the authority cannot keep it running.

case_name: Urmila Kumari Kadam v. Y.B. Builders Pvt. Ltd. & Nimai Developers
citation: Appeal No. 696 of 2026, Haryana REAT, order dated 31 August 2026, reported as 2026 LLBiz REAT (HR) 62
holding_summary: A homebuyer who paid half her flat's price without ever signing a Builder Buyer Agreement found out, on appeal, that the absence of that agreement was not the problem with her case. The Haryana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal has rejected her claim for delayed-possession charges on a narrower ground: the promoter had offered her possession before the contractual due date arrived. Urmila Kumari Kadam had bought a unit in the Nimai Palace project from Y.B. Builders Pvt. Ltd. and Nimai Developers for a total consideration of Rs 67,37,923, of which she had paid Rs 50 lakh. No formal Builder Buyer Agreement was ever executed between the parties, which is often, by itself, a point of vulnerability for a promoter in RERA proceedings. Here it did not matter, because the Tribunal's decision turned on a different sequence of dates entirely. Working from whatever documentation did exist, the due date for possession was calculated as 11 June 2023. The promoters had made their offer of possession on 1 April 2023, more than two months ahead of that due date. The project's paperwork showed an Occupation Certificate granted in principle on 10 February 2023, with the final Occupation Certificate following on 12 April 2023, just eleven days after the possession offer itself.
why_it_matters: Homebuyers pursuing delayed-possession compensation under RERA should check the exact due date fixed by their allotment, not just whether the Occupation Certificate preceded the possession offer, since the Haryana Appellate Tribunal has treated an offer made before the due date as valid even where it came close in time to, or ahead of, the final Occupation Certificate. Promoters without a signed Builder Buyer Agreement can still defeat a delay claim if they can independently establish an early due date and a possession offer that beat it.
title: Offer of Possession Made Before the Due Date Bars a Delay Claim, Holds Haryana RERA Appellate Tribunal
