meta_description: Haryana REAT holds a promoter's possession offer made before the contractual due date defeats a homebuyer's claim for delayed-possession interest.
card_tip: When assessing a delayed-possession claim, compare the offer date against the fixed due date first; the gap to the final Occupation Certificate may not be decisive.

case_name: Rekha Saxena and Anr. v. Roman Catholic Diocese Allahabad Pvt. Ltd. Thru Director General, The Bishop
citation: (2026) 09 AHC CK 4243, Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench, appeal under Order XLIII Rule 1(r) CPC from an order of the Civil Judge (Senior Division), Raebareli
holding_summary: Owning a decree that cancels someone else's sale deed is not the same as owning the right to throw that person out of the house. The Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench made that distinction count for a woman who had lived in her home for 38 years, even though the deed her possession traced back to had long since been judicially cancelled. The underlying dispute began decades earlier with a registered power of attorney executed in favour of one Augustine Paul. That power of attorney was purportedly cancelled, though the revocation came to be registered only some days after the cancellation itself. In the gap between the two dates, Augustine Paul went ahead and executed a sale deed in favour of Savitri Srivastava, who was the mother-in-law of the first appellant, Rekha Saxena. The sale deed, in other words, was executed in a window where the seller's authority to act was already in question, which is precisely what the Roman Catholic Diocese of Allahabad later challenged in the civil suit that followed. That suit was decreed ex-parte as far back as 21 April 2001, but the decree itself was formally drawn up only on 7 April 2023, more than two decades later. What the decree actually said mattered a great deal to the appeal. It cancelled the 1987 sale deed and restrained further construction on the property. It contained no direction at all for eviction, and no order for delivery of possession to the decree-holder.
why_it_matters: A decree-holder who has only secured cancellation of a sale deed, without a specific direction for eviction or delivery of possession, cannot use that decree to dispossess the person in occupation, however long after the original transaction the cancellation comes. Anyone in long, settled possession of property whose underlying title document has been cancelled by a court can still resist forcible dispossession and seek an injunction until the decree-holder obtains a proper order for possession through due process.
title: A Decree Cancelling a Sale Deed Does Not Authorise Eviction on Its Own, Rules Allahabad High Court
meta_description: Allahabad HC's Lucknow Bench holds a decree that only cancels a sale deed cannot be used to evict a 38-year occupant without a specific possession order.
card_tip: Before acting on a decree that cancels a sale deed, check whether it also directs eviction; if not, you cannot dispossess the occupant without a separate order.

case_name: Anjaniputra Ispat Ltd. v. IAG Company Ltd.
citation: Company Appeal (AT) No. 39 of 2026 with connected Company Appeal (AT)(Ins) No. 1874 of 2025, NCLAT Principal Bench, decided September 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: An appellant who files late under one statute sometimes tries to switch tracks to another, hoping a fresh provision buys a fresh limitation clock without losing the benefit of the time already spent litigating. The NCLAT's Principal Bench has shut that door, at least for a litigant who tried converting a time-barred Section 61 appeal under the IBC into a Section 421 appeal under the Companies Act. The order under challenge was passed by the NCLT on 8 September 2025. An appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was filed on 20 November 2025, which worked out to the 76th day after the order, well past the 30-day limitation period and the further 15-day maximum condonable extension that Section 61(2) allows. That delay alone put the Section 61 appeal in serious jeopardy from the outset. Rather than let that appeal be dismissed outright, the appellant sought liberty from the Tribunal, which was granted on 29 January 2026. The Tribunal's order contemplated the appellant amending the existing Section 61 memorandum of appeal and converting it into one framed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, a provision governing appeals from NCLT orders generally. Instead of amending the existing appeal paper, the appellant filed what amounted to a fresh Section 421 appeal on 30 January 2026, a day after the liberty was granted.
why_it_matters: Where a tribunal grants liberty to convert a time-barred Section 61 IBC appeal into a Section 421 Companies Act appeal, counsel must amend the existing appeal memorandum rather than file a fresh appeal, since a fresh filing resets the limitation clock under Section 421(3) and forfeits any benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act for time spent on the earlier proceeding. Getting this procedural choice wrong can leave an otherwise meritorious appeal dismissed purely on limitation.
title: Converting an IBC Appeal Into a Companies Act Appeal Does Not Rescue a Time-Barred Case, Rules NCLAT
meta_description: NCLAT holds switching a Section 61 IBC appeal into a Section 421 appeal counts as a fresh filing for limitation, dismissing it as time-barred.
card_tip: If a tribunal allows converting a Section 61 IBC appeal into a Section 421 appeal, file it as an amendment, not a fresh appeal, or the limitation clock resets against you.

case_name: Deyzeel Aggarwal v. InterGlobe Aviation Ltd.
citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), Delhi, order reported 16 September 2026
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), Delhi
holding_summary: A passenger who shows up before his rescheduled departure time should not be the one penalised when the airline's own records fail to catch up with its own reschedule. A Delhi consumer commission has said exactly that to IndiGo, finding the airline liable after it marked a traveller a no-show despite his having turned up ahead of the delayed departure it had itself notified him of. The complainant, Deyzeel Aggarwal, was booked on a Delhi to Bengaluru flight. IndiGo sent him an SMS and an email informing him that the flight had been delayed for operational reasons and moved to a 4:00 PM departure. Relying on that communication, Aggarwal reached the airport counter at 2:45 PM, well ahead of the newly notified departure time. IndiGo nonetheless treated him as a No Show, citing his failure to meet mandatory check-in timelines, and refused to let him board. Delhi's District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I, North District, found that conduct amounted to both deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice. An airline that sends a passenger a reschedule notice cannot then fall back on check-in deadlines calculated from the original, superseded schedule to deny him boarding when he arrives in good time against the schedule it actually communicated to him.
why_it_matters: Airlines cannot rely on Conditions of Carriage as a blanket defence when a passenger follows the airline's own reschedule notice and is still denied boarding for allegedly missing check-in deadlines calculated against the original, superseded schedule. The ruling gives consumer forums a basis to look past standard-form airline contracts and apply statutory consumer protection remedies directly, strengthening the hand of passengers caught out by airlines' internal scheduling or communication failures.
title: IndiGo Held Liable for Denying Boarding After It Rescheduled the Flight, Rules Delhi Consumer Commission
meta_description: Delhi consumer commission finds IndiGo liable for marking a passenger a no-show after rescheduling his flight, rejecting its Carriage defence.
card_tip: If an airline reschedules your flight and still denies boarding, keep that SMS or email; a commission can treat it as overriding the Conditions of Carriage on check-in timing.

case_name: Commissioner of Service Tax, Mumbai v. M/s Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
citation: Civil Appeal Nos. 2471-2473 of 2015, 2026 INSC 723, decided 20 July 2026
holding_summary: Two of the country's largest oil marketing companies have spent over a decade arguing that selling CNG from their own pumps was simply their own business of selling fuel. The Supreme Court has now told Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum that, for the years in question, it was not their fuel to sell in that sense at all; they were acting as commission agents for Mahanagar Gas Limited, and that distinction costs them a service tax bill running past Rs 16 crore. The dispute covers the period from April 2005 to March 2011, during which BPCL and HPCL distributed CNG to retail customers in Mumbai on behalf of Mahanagar Gas, the city gas distribution company that actually held the supply arrangements and infrastructure. The tax department's case was that this distribution arrangement fit squarely within Business Auxiliary Service under Section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994, a category that captures services rendered on behalf of a client, including the kind of agency function BPCL and HPCL were performing for MGL. Both companies had won before the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, which set aside the demands in June 2014 on the view that distributing CNG through their own retail outlets was an ordinary sale transaction on their own account, not a service rendered to MGL as a client. That characterisation, if it had survived, would have kept the transactions outside the service tax net entirely for those years, since a sale of goods and a taxable service are treated very differently under the statute.
why_it_matters: Companies distributing another entity's goods through their own retail network, even while billing and dealing directly with end customers, can still be treated as commission agents liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary Service if the upstream principal retains control over pricing, title and commercial risk. The ruling revives a decade-old, Rs 16.68 crore demand against BPCL and HPCL and signals that CESTAT's earlier, more retailer-friendly reading of such distribution arrangements will not automatically survive Supreme Court scrutiny.
title: BPCL and HPCL Liable as Commission Agents for CNG Sales to Mahanagar Gas, Rules Supreme Court
meta_description: Supreme Court revives a Rs 16.68 crore service tax demand against BPCL and HPCL, holding their CNG distribution for Mahanagar Gas was agency service.
card_tip: Before treating a distribution arrangement as your own sale, check who fixes the price, holds title and bears commercial risk; that allocation decides the service tax position.

case_name: Maternal Grandparents v. Biological Father (parties not named in available reporting)
citation: D.B. Civil Misc. Appeal, Rajasthan High Court, Jodhpur Bench, decided on or about 6-7 October 2026 (case number not available in the reporting reviewed)
holding_summary: A seven-year-old boy who has spent his whole life in his grandparents' home was not, the Rajasthan High Court held, a prize that passes automatically to his biological father merely because the father carries the stronger paper claim. A Division Bench of Justices Munnuri Laxman and Sangeeta Sharma, sitting at the Jodhpur Bench, set aside a Family Court order of January 2025 that had awarded the father full custody, and replaced it with a staged arrangement that for now keeps the boy with his maternal grandparents. The grandparents had raised the child from infancy, while the father's presence in his life had been limited enough that the bench found no real bond existed between them. Their appeal argued that the Family Court had treated the father's legal status as guardian as effectively decisive, without weighing what an abrupt transfer would do to a child who knew only one home. The bench agreed that the lower court had got the balance wrong. Running through the judgment is a line the Rajasthan High Court has applied in custody matters before: a natural guardian's right to custody is a legal entitlement, not an automatic trump card, and it yields wherever the child's welfare points the other way. Here the two pulled in different directions. The father had the stronger entitlement on paper. The child's welfare, built over seven years of daily life with his grandparents, pointed firmly at keeping that continuity intact, at least for now.
why_it_matters: Family lawyers advising grandparents, relatives, or step-parents who have raised a child should treat this as confirmation that a settled, long-term bond with a caregiver can outweigh a biological parent's bare legal right to custody, at least until a real relationship is rebuilt. The phased-access model the bench adopted, rather than an all-or-nothing transfer, offers a template worth citing in custody disputes where the legal guardian has been largely absent from the child's actual upbringing.
title: A Settled Bond With Grandparents Beats a Father's Bare Legal Right to Custody, Rules Rajasthan High Court
meta_description: Rajasthan High Court sets aside a Family Court order handing a boy to his father, keeps him with grandparents, orders only phased access.
card_tip: In custody disputes against an absentee legal guardian, lead with evidence of the child's existing bond and the disruption a sudden transfer would cause, not just the guardian's weaker paper claim.

case_name: Haryana Power Purchase Centre v. Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd. (arising from proceedings before the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission)
citation: Appeal before APTEL against HERC's order in Petition No. 78 of 2025, decided 18 September 2026 (APTEL appeal number not available in the reporting reviewed)
holding_summary: A solar developer who let one adverse order stand without appeal found out, two petitions and two years later, that the issue it thought it could reopen had already been closed for good. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity has set aside a Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission order that had revived Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd.'s claim to a higher tariff for its 5 MW plant, holding that the point was res judicata. The dispute traces back to a 2024 petition, Petition No. 26 of 2024, in which Siwana asked HERC to restore a tariff of Rs 6.44 per kWh and to pay the difference over the Rs 5.68 rate it had actually been receiving. HERC dismissed that petition on 12 November 2024, holding the claim barred by res judicata. Siwana did not appeal that dismissal. Instead, in 2025 Siwana filed a fresh petition, Petition No. 78 of 2025, seeking substantially the same relief dressed up differently. This time HERC took a different view of its own earlier order. In May 2026 it held that an earlier settlement between the parties covered only dues up to March 2019, and on that reasoning it directed the Haryana Power Purchase Centre to pay Siwana Rs 6.44 per kWh prospectively, along with the differential amount and interest at 9.15 percent. The Haryana Power Purchase Centre appealed that order to APTEL.
why_it_matters: Power sector developers and distribution utilities should treat an unappealed regulatory order as genuinely final: APTEL has confirmed that res judicata bars a fresh petition seeking the same relief years later, even where the regulator itself later takes a more sympathetic view of the facts. Counsel should advise clients to exhaust appeal rights promptly rather than relitigating a settled tariff question through a differently framed petition.
title: A Tariff Dispute You Already Lost and Didn't Appeal Stays Lost, Holds APTEL in Haryana Solar Case
meta_description: APTEL sets aside an HERC order reviving a solar developer's tariff claim, holding the issue was already settled by an unchallenged 2024 order.
card_tip: Treat an unappealed regulatory order as final; a fresh petition seeking the same relief on a repackaged theory will not survive appeal even if the regulator first grants it.

case_name: State of Gujarat v. Chimanbhai Bhanubhai Chaudhari & Ors.
citation: R/CR.A/918/2008, 2026:GUJHC:40381, Gujarat High Court, decided 17 June 2026
holding_summary: Sweet shops across India have coated kaju katli in a thin layer of edible silver or aluminium foil for decades without a second thought from most customers. When a food inspector in Gujarat decided that foil coating amounted to adulteration, the dispute over one batch of kaju katli ended up running for close to two decades before the Gujarat High Court closed it for good. The prosecution began with a food inspector's sample of kaju katli coated in aluminium foil, seized from the accused's shop and sent for analysis under the adulteration law then in force. A trial followed, and at some stage of these proceedings the conviction that had been recorded against the accused was reversed on appeal, well before the matter reached the High Court. The State, dissatisfied with that reversal, filed a criminal appeal under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, arguing that the acquittal was contrary to law and to the evidence on record. Justice Hemant M. Prachchhak, hearing the State's appeal as a single judge, confirmed the acquittal and gave two independent reasons for doing so. The first went to the heart of what adulteration actually requires. Per LiveLaw's report of the judgment, the court found no evidence on record that aluminium foil used as a coating was injurious to health or rendered the sweet unfit for human consumption. Using a coating that nobody could show was harmful did not, by itself, make the kaju katli adulterated.
why_it_matters: Food businesses facing adulteration charges over coatings, additives, or ingredients in long-accepted use should know that Indian courts require actual proof of harm, not a bare allegation that a substance was not expressly authorised. Equally, any defect in the sampling procedure, however procedural it may look, can independently defeat a prosecution, so defence counsel should scrutinise sample-collection testimony as closely as the substantive adulteration charge itself.
title: Coating Kaju Katli in Aluminium Foil Isn't Adulteration Without Proof of Harm, Holds Gujarat High Court
meta_description: Gujarat High Court confirms an acquittal over foil-coated kaju katli, citing no proof the foil was injurious and a flawed sampling procedure.
card_tip: In adulteration prosecutions, press on both fronts: demand proof the substance is actually harmful, and scrutinise whether the sample bottle and collection procedure met basic protocol.

case_name: Ramamurthy v. Rajendran
citation: O.P. No. 69 of 2012, with connected A.Nos. 3416, 3417, 3419 of 2026 & 4268 of 2023, Madras High Court, decided 24 September 2026
holding_summary: A property dispute tied to the estate of former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.G. Ramachandran has been running in one form or another since the 1990s, and the Madras High Court has just closed one more front of it. Heirs of MGR's brother, M.G. Chakrapani, had sought Letters of Administration over a property in Virugambakkam, Chennai, arguing that MGR had died intestate as to this particular asset. Justice A.D. Maria Clete rejected that claim outright. The petition was old even by the standards of estate litigation. O.P. No. 69 of 2012 had sat on the Original Side docket for well over a decade, with connected applications, A.Nos. 3416, 3417 and 3419 of 2026 along with A.No. 4268 of 2023, filed along the way as the Chakrapani heirs pressed their claim. Their theory was narrow but, if accepted, would have reopened a slice of MGR's estate that everyone else had treated as settled for more than thirty years: they argued that because MGR's will did not specifically dispose of the Virugambakkam property, he had died intestate as to that asset, and intestate succession should apply to it instead. The court's answer turned on a document that was never really in dispute: MGR's will, dated 18 January 1987. That will had already been probated by the Madras High Court itself, back in 1992. Justice Clete held that the Virugambakkam property was in fact covered by the terms of that 1987 will, which meant there was no gap in the testamentary disposition for intestate succession to fill. The probate granted decades earlier was not something the Chakrapani heirs could get around simply by arguing, now, that one particular property had somehow been left out of it.
why_it_matters: Heirs considering a Letters of Administration petition against an estate that has already been through probate should first establish, with real certainty, that the specific asset they are chasing falls outside the probated will's terms. This ruling confirms that an Indian court will not revisit a decades-old probate order property by property simply because a later claimant argues the will left a particular asset undisposed.
title: A Will Probated in 1992 Still Governs the Property, Madras High Court Tells MGR's Brother's Heirs in 2026
meta_description: Madras High Court rejects a Letters of Administration claim by MGR's brother's heirs, holding MGR's probated 1987 will already covers the property.
card_tip: Before filing a Letters of Administration petition against a probated estate, confirm the asset actually falls outside the will's terms; probate forecloses intestacy claims asset by asset.

case_name: Aroha Labs Pte. Ltd. v. Prem Dharmani & Ors.
citation: AP.IM. No. 4 of 2026, Karnataka High Court, decided on or about early August 2026 (reported 3 August 2026)
holding_summary: A Singapore company that agreed to arbitrate its disputes in Singapore might expect an Indian court to have nothing to say about those disputes until the arbitral tribunal has ruled. The Karnataka High Court has now confirmed, in a dispute between Aroha Labs Pte. Ltd. and a group of former consultants, that this expectation is wrong where interim relief is concerned. Aroha Labs, a Singapore-based technology company, had entered into master service agreements with a set of independent consultants between May 2024 and November 2025 to build several software applications, including an astrology app called Astro 247. A dispute later arose over who actually owned the applications once the working relationship broke down. A related Indian company, Creato Club Private Limited, was incorporated along the way, and Aroha Labs alleged that Creato Club began asserting ownership over the applications and went so far as to file a civil suit against Aroha and its directors before the Bangalore Civil Courts. The underlying commercial agreements provided for arbitration seated in Singapore under the Singapore International Arbitration Centre's rules. Aroha Labs nonetheless approached the Karnataka High Court under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking interim protection, specifically restraining the former consultants and the entities linked to Creato Club from dealing with the disputed applications while the Singapore arbitration ran its course.
why_it_matters: Businesses drafting arbitration clauses with a foreign seat should not assume this keeps Indian courts out of the picture; without an express exclusion, a party can still obtain interim relief under Section 9 over assets, data, or IP situated in India while a foreign-seated arbitration is pending. Counsel structuring such agreements should address this expressly if exclusion of Indian court jurisdiction, including for interim measures, is actually intended.
title: Picking Singapore as Your Arbitration Seat Doesn't Shut Indian Courts Out of Interim Relief, Rules Karnataka High Court
meta_description: Karnataka High Court grants interim relief despite a Singapore-seated arbitration, holding a foreign seat alone does not oust Indian courts' jurisdiction.
card_tip: If a cross-border arbitration agreement is meant to exclude Indian courts even for interim relief, say so expressly; a foreign seat alone will not achieve that exclusion.

case_name: Polycab India Limited v. Asier Metals (arising from Asier Metals' Section 9 petition against Polycab India Limited)
citation: Appeal against NCLT Ahmedabad's order in C.P.(IB) No. 273/9/AHM/2026, NCLAT Principal Bench, New Delhi, stay order dated 9 October 2026 (appeal number not available in the reporting reviewed)
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: A dispute over invoices worth less than three crore rupees put one of India's largest wire and cable manufacturers briefly inside the insolvency process, before the appellate tribunal pulled it back out again within two days. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal has stayed an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting Polycab India Limited into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process on a Section 9 petition filed by Asier Metals. Asier Metals had approached the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, alleging an operational debt default by Polycab. Reports differ slightly on the exact figure, with most putting it at around Rs 2.79 crore and at least one source citing Rs 2.78 crore. The NCLT admitted the petition and commenced CIRP against Polycab, a decision the company moved immediately to challenge on appeal. Polycab's defence to the underlying claim rests on how its invoicing worked. The company says the disputed invoices were marked 'Provisional Billing' and remained subject to final pricing, reconciliation, quantity discounts, credit notes, and other adjustments, meaning the amount Asier Metals claimed as due was never a fixed, undisputed sum in the first place. The NCLT, in admitting the petition, evidently found no pre-existing dispute of the kind that would have barred admission under the settled Mobilox standard for operational debt claims.
why_it_matters: Corporate debtors facing an operational debt claim built on provisional or reconciliation-pending invoices should raise and document that dispute clearly before the NCLT at the admission stage, since the Mobilox pre-existing dispute standard is applied there and an admission, once made, can trigger exchange-level consequences that an appellate stay does not automatically undo. Creditors, meanwhile, should expect well-resourced corporate debtors to secure a conditional stay quickly even after admission.
title: NCLAT Stays Polycab's Insolvency Admission Over a ₹2.79 Crore Dispute, Conditional on a Full Deposit
meta_description: NCLAT stays an NCLT order admitting Polycab India into insolvency on Asier Metals' claim, conditional on Polycab depositing the disputed amount.
card_tip: Document a provisional-billing or reconciliation-pending dispute before the NCLT at the admission stage; a later appellate stay will not reverse exchange-level consequences already triggered.

case_name: Ramegowdu Mahendra v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax
citation: W.P. No. 32056 of 2026, Madras High Court, decided 20 August 2026
holding_summary: A taxpayer who found his income tax reassessment notice built almost entirely on a GST adjudication order he was still appealing has got the Madras High Court to say, in principle, that this is not how reassessment is supposed to work, even though the notice itself survives for now. Ramegowdu Mahendra challenged a notice issued under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act on 27 May 2026, seeking to reopen his assessment for Assessment Year 2023-24. The notice traced back to a GST adjudication order dated 3 February 2025, which Mahendra had separately appealed. He argued before the High Court that a deemed stay applied to that GST order given the pending appeal, and that the Income Tax Department had simply lifted its reassessment case from an adjudication that was itself still contested and unresolved. Justice Senthilkumar Ramamoorthy agreed with the underlying principle. The court held that any reassessment has to be carried out in compliance with the applicable provisions of the Income Tax Act in its own right, and that the income tax authorities cannot ride piggyback on an adjudication made under GST law. A finding reached in a GST proceeding, on its own, is not a substitute for the independent satisfaction the Income Tax Act requires before a reassessment can proceed.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers facing a Section 148 reassessment notice that leans on a parallel GST adjudication should preserve this objection even where a High Court declines to quash the notice at the threshold stage; the real test comes when the reassessment order itself is passed, since it must rest on an independent income tax analysis rather than simply importing the GST adjudication's conclusions.
title: Income Tax Cannot Ride Piggyback on a GST Order to Justify Reassessment, Says Madras High Court
meta_description: Madras High Court holds income tax reassessment cannot rest solely on a GST adjudication order, though it declines to quash the notice at this early stage.
card_tip: Where a reassessment notice leans on a GST order, raise the independence objection now and save it for the final reassessment order, since the notice alone is unlikely to be quashed on that ground.

case_name: IFCI Limited v. Hotel Mythri & Anr.
citation: OP(C) No. 2569 of 2026, Kerala High Court, decided 15 September 2026
holding_summary: A lessee who lost a securitisation application before the Debt Recovery Tribunal did not get a second chance to raise the same grievance by dressing it up as a civil suit for an injunction, the Kerala High Court has held, closing off a workaround that tenants caught up in a landlord's loan default sometimes try. IFCI Limited held a registered mortgage over the property in question as the secured creditor. While that mortgage subsisted, the mortgagor executed a registered lease deed in favour of Hotel Mythri for a term of nine years. When IFCI moved to enforce its security under the SARFAESI Act, Hotel Mythri resisted, filing S.A. No. 174 of 2020 before the Debt Recovery Tribunal-II, Ernakulam, asking the DRT to examine its position as lessee against the secured creditor's enforcement steps. The DRT dismissed that securitisation application on 5 December 2024, rejecting Hotel Mythri's claim. Rather than appeal that order to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal, Hotel Mythri instead filed a fresh civil suit before the Sub Court, Nedumangad, this time seeking a prohibitory injunction restraining IFCI from taking any further steps under the SARFAESI Act and from evicting Hotel Mythri by invoking Section 14 of that Act. The Sub Court declined to reject IFCI's objection to the plaint outright, and IFCI took that refusal up to the Kerala High Court.
why_it_matters: Secured creditors facing a lessee or occupant who has already lost a securitisation challenge before the DRT should cite this ruling immediately if that party tries a fresh civil suit raising the same grievance; Section 35 of the SARFAESI Act and ordinary res judicata principles bar that second attempt. Prospective lessees of mortgaged property should also treat a lease taken without the mortgagee's consent as offering limited protection against enforcement under Section 65A of the Transfer of Property Act.
title: Lose Before the DRT and You Cannot Try the Same SARFAESI Grievance Again in a Civil Suit, Rules Kerala High Court
meta_description: Kerala High Court rejects a lessee's civil suit against a SARFAESI action, holding it barred by Section 35 and res judicata after an adverse DRT order.
card_tip: If a lessee or occupant has already lost a Section 17 SARFAESI challenge before the DRT, raise Section 35 and res judicata immediately against any fresh civil suit covering the same ground.

case_name: Omaxe Limited & Ors. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India
citation: (2026) 09 SEBI CK 4384, Securities Appellate Tribunal, order dated 1 September 2026, dismissing the appeal against SEBI's order dated 30 July 2024
holding_summary: Two years after SEBI accused real estate developer Omaxe Limited of running roughly Rs 647 crore through a series of related-party transactions it called fraudulent, the Securities Appellate Tribunal has had its say, and it did not mince words. The tribunal dismissed Omaxe's appeal in full, describing the transactions under scrutiny as a series of fraudulent 'make believe' financial transactions. The appeal challenged a SEBI order dated 30 July 2024 that had barred Omaxe Limited, its chairman Rohtas Goel, managing director Mohit Goel, and several other noticees from accessing the securities market for two years. The SEBI order went further than a market ban alone: it also prohibited the individual noticees covered by the order from serving as directors or key managerial personnel of any listed company, and it imposed monetary penalties on top of both restrictions. SEBI's underlying finding was that Omaxe had engaged in round-tripping, cycling roughly Rs 647 crore through transactions structured to look legitimate on paper but lacking any genuine commercial substance. The tribunal's own language leaves little doubt about how it read the evidence. According to LiveLaw Biz's report of the order, the bench held that the alleged violation of the Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices Regulations was, in its words, largely writ on the face of each transaction, and it went on to reject Omaxe's separate plea for a more lenient view on the monetary penalties imposed.
why_it_matters: Listed companies and their promoters structuring related-party or intra-group transactions should treat SAT's willingness to call such dealings fraudulent 'make believe' transactions as a signal that the tribunal will look past documentary form to commercial substance when SEBI alleges round-tripping under the PFUTP Regulations. A SAT dismissal does not end the dispute if a Supreme Court appeal follows, but it does restore the original market ban and director disqualification in full pending any such appeal.
title: SAT Calls Omaxe's ₹647 Crore Transactions 'Make Believe', Upholds SEBI's Two-Year Market Ban
meta_description: SAT dismisses Omaxe's appeal against SEBI's market ban over alleged ₹647 crore round-tripping, calling the deals sham transactions.
card_tip: When defending related-party deals against a round-tripping claim, focus on real commercial substance; SAT looks past documentary form once a PFUTP violation appears evident on the transactions.

case_name: BRD Finance Ltd. v. Santhosh P. & Anr.
citation: RSA No. 194 of 2026, decided 10 August 2026
holding_summary: BRD Finance Ltd, a kuri company that runs chit schemes in Kerala, sued Santhosh P before the Munsiff Court at Chavakkad to recover about Rs 3.47 lakh due on a promissory note. Nothing unusual about that, until the Kerala government stepped in halfway through the litigation and changed which court was allowed to hear it. On 24 February 2020, while the suit was still pending, the State notified all Sub Courts in Kerala as Commercial Courts for the purpose of hearing commercial disputes of a specified value, which under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 then stood at anything above Rs 3 lakh. BRD Finance's claim, at Rs 3.47 lakh, fell squarely inside that bracket. Nobody flagged the point. The Munsiff Court carried on, heard the suit on its merits, and dismissed it. BRD Finance appealed to the Sub Court at Chavakkad, which upheld the dismissal, again without anyone raising the jurisdiction question. It was only in second appeal before the Kerala High Court that BRD Finance argued, for the first time, that both courts below had acted without jurisdiction. Justice Easwaran S. agreed, and did not treat the lateness of the objection as a bar. The notification creating Commercial Courts had taken the power to decide specified-value commercial disputes away from ordinary civil courts, including the Munsiff Court, from the date it came into force. A decree passed by a court that no longer had that power is not voidable at the choice of a party who forgets to object; it is void, and a void decree can be pointed out at any stage, including for the first time in second appeal.
why_it_matters: Any pending civil suit that crosses a state's Commercial Courts pecuniary threshold can be sitting in the wrong forum without anyone noticing, and this ruling confirms that the resulting judgment is void, not merely irregular, however late the objection surfaces. Litigants and their counsel need to check, at the first hearing after any Commercial Courts notification, whether their suit should have been transferred, rather than assume a decree on merits has settled the matter.
title: Civil Court's Merits Ruling on a Specified-Value Dispute Was Void Once Commercial Courts Were Notified: Kerala HC
meta_description: Kerala High Court voids a Munsiff Court decree, holding civil courts lose jurisdiction over specified-value disputes once Commercial Courts are designated.
card_tip: Check pending recovery suits against the state's Commercial Courts notification and threshold; a decree from the wrong forum is void and challengeable at any stage.

case_name: Alpro Industries & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
citation: W.P.(C) 12818/2026, decided 30 September 2026
holding_summary: Indo Alusys Industries Limited sued Alpro Industries in 2016 to recover about Rs 35.50 lakh with interest. At the time, a commercial dispute only went to a Commercial Court if it was worth at least Rs 1 crore, so the suit was filed and tried as an ordinary civil suit. Two years later, the Commercial Courts (Amendment) Act, 2018 cut that threshold down to Rs 3 lakh, which meant a case like this one would, if filed afresh, have gone straight to a Commercial Court. By the time the suit had dragged on to reach the evidence stage, Alpro Industries saw an opening. It applied to have the matter transferred to a Commercial Court, presumably hoping for the procedural advantages, or at least a materially different trajectory, that the specialised forum offers. The trial court refused. Section 19 of the 2018 Amendment Act confines the lower threshold to commercial disputes instituted on or after 3 May 2018, the date the amendment came into force, and this suit had been instituted in 2016. Rather than simply accept that answer and move on, Alpro Industries challenged Section 19 itself before the Delhi High Court, arguing that drawing the line at 3 May 2018 was arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution. Two similarly placed litigants, one whose suit happened to be filed a week before the cut-off and one a week after, would be treated completely differently for no principled reason, the petitioner said, and a provision that produces that kind of accidental inequality cannot survive constitutional scrutiny.
why_it_matters: Businesses with suits pending from before May 2018 sometimes assume a later fall in the specified-value threshold lets them switch to a Commercial Court mid-litigation; this ruling forecloses that strategy and confirms the forum is locked in by the date of institution. Counsel advising on long-pending commercial suits should stop pursuing transfer applications on this ground and focus on the ordinary appellate route instead.
title: Delhi HC Upholds Section 19 of the 2018 Commercial Courts Amendment, Rejects Article 14 Challenge to Its Cut-Off Date
meta_description: Delhi High Court dismisses a challenge to Section 19 of the Commercial Courts Amendment, holding its prospective cut-off does not violate Article 14.
card_tip: Stop filing transfer applications to move pre-3 May 2018 suits into Commercial Courts on the lowered threshold; Section 19's prospective application is now upheld as constitutional.

case_name: U.P. State Highways Authority v. M/s Abhijeet Meerut Karnal Toll Road Limited
citation: Section 37 Appeal No. 41 of 2025, 2026 LLBiz HC (ALL) 58, decided 23 July 2026
holding_summary: A concession agreement signed on 16 December 2011 handed the four-laning of State Highway 82 to Abhijeet Meerut Karnal Toll Road Limited, on a design, build, finance, operate and transfer basis. The deal depended on the Authority clearing 90 per cent of the right of way before the concessionaire had to perform its side. Instead, the Authority issued only a Section 4 notification under the Land Acquisition Act and never followed through with the Section 6 declaration that would have actually vested the land. Years passed with the project effectively stalled. On 13 January 2014, the concessionaire pulled the plug and terminated the agreement, blaming the Authority's failure to deliver possession. The dispute went to arbitration, and the tribunal split. A majority of the panel found the Authority in breach and awarded loss of profits, though it scaled the figure down sharply from the concessionaire's claim of Rs 640.50 crore to Rs 157.57 crore, largely built on a financial model projecting what the concession would have earned over its term. The majority also awarded Rs 25.53 crore to cover payments the concessionaire owed its own EPC contractor. The presiding arbitrator dissented on both heads, taking the view that the loss-of-profits claim was too speculative to sustain. Challenging the award under Section 34 before the Commercial Court got the Authority nowhere, so it appealed further under Section 37 to the Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench. Its central argument was that a financial projection, standing alone, cannot support an award of this size; without independent corroborating evidence such as actual toll collections on comparable stretches, cost records, or traffic studies tested at trial, the model is just an exercise in assumptions dressed up as damages.
why_it_matters: Arbitral tribunals award large loss-of-profits figures in PPP termination disputes based substantially on financial models, and authorities routinely challenge those awards without success given the narrow scope of Sections 34 and 37. This ruling shows a model-only damages case is vulnerable even on that narrow review, so concessionaires pursuing termination claims should build an evidentiary record beyond the projections themselves.
title: Allahabad HC Severs ₹157.57 Crore Loss-of-Profits Award Against UP Highways Authority, Upholds Rest of Arbitral Award
meta_description: Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench partly sets aside a PPP award against U.P. State Highways Authority, severing an unproven loss-of-profits claim.
card_tip: In PPP termination arbitrations, back any loss-of-profits claim with evidence beyond the financial model, such as cost records, or risk losing that head of damages on a Section 37 appeal.

case_name: Petitioner (landowner) v. National Highways Authority of India & State of Bihar (parties not fully named in available reporting)
citation: CWJC No. 10512 of 2026, decided 28 July 2026
holding_summary: National Highway 527C needed land from a petitioner in Bihar, and NHAI sent him a communication telling him, in effect, to act on it. The trouble was that the communication carried no letter number, no date, and no description of which land it concerned or how much of it. The petitioner could not have complied with it even if he had wanted to, because it did not say what compliance required. He had built on the part of his holding that remained unacquired, and the blank notice left him worried that NHAI or the district administration would treat it as a valid demand and move against his structures without ever telling him precisely what land they claimed and on what basis. With no reference number to track and no description of the land at stake, he had no way of knowing what response, if any, the notice actually called for. He approached the Patna High Court seeking protection against any such action until a proper demarcation was carried out. Before Justice Rajiv Roy, both the State and NHAI did something that single judges in land acquisition matters do not often get from either side: they conceded the obvious. The State and NHAI fairly acknowledged that the communication could not be treated as a valid notice at all. There was no serious attempt to defend the document on its own terms, because it could not be defended; a notice that omits its own reference number, date and the extent of land it purports to cover fails at the threshold, before any question of compliance or limitation even arises.
why_it_matters: National highway projects routinely rely on individual notices to landowners at various stages of acquisition, and this ruling confirms courts will not let a defective notice, whether blank or missing altogether, stand as the basis for any coercive action against a landowner's structures or claims. Project authorities need to treat notice drafting as a compliance step with real consequences, not paperwork, since both the notice and the official who issued it can be held to account.
title: A Notice With No Number, No Date and No Land Details Is No Notice at All: Patna HC Fines NHAI ₹5,000
meta_description: Patna High Court orders NHAI to issue a proper notice and demarcate a landowner's plot after both NHAI and the State admitted the earlier notice was blank.
card_tip: Before acting on a highway land notice, check it names a specific parcel and carries a reference number and date; one missing these basics can be treated as no notice at all.

case_name: ANI Media Private Limited v. RSY News & Anr.
citation: CS(COMM) 1018/2024, 2026:DHC:8749, decided 29 September 2026
holding_summary: ANI, the news agency that licenses its footage to broadcasters across the country, found twelve of its videos sitting on four YouTube channels run by RSY News, uploaded between August and October 2024. It sued for copyright infringement, naming Google LLC as a co-defendant because the videos lived on YouTube's platform, and sought a permanent injunction, takedown of the offending URLs, damages of Rs 2,00,00,500, and a public acknowledgment that RSY News had copied its work without permission. RSY News never showed up to defend itself. Despite service of summons, it filed no written statement and made no appearance through the life of the suit. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav proceeded to decide the matter without its participation, examining ANI's video content side by side with what RSY News had uploaded to determine whether a defence of fair dealing for reporting current events, the exception news organisations most commonly invoke when they use each other's footage, could have saved the uploads even if RSY News had bothered to raise it. It could not. The Court's comparison found that in ten of the twelve disputed videos, RSY News had reproduced ANI's footage entirely, or so close to entirely that the difference was immaterial. This was not a case of a few seconds of B-roll lifted to illustrate a separate report, or a clip used as supporting visual evidence while a reporter's own commentary carried the substance of the piece. The uploads functioned as straight substitutes for ANI's original videos, available on RSY News's own channels in place of, rather than alongside, independent reporting.
why_it_matters: News and digital media outlets frequently lean on the fair dealing exception to justify reusing competitors' footage, assuming any connection to reporting current events will cover them; this ruling draws a clear line that reproducing footage whole, as a substitute for the original rather than in support of independent reporting, falls outside that exception regardless of the current-events label attached to it. Platforms hosting such content also remain exposed to enforceable takedown directions once infringement is established.
title: Reproducing News Footage Whole Is Not Fair Dealing Even for Reporting Current Events: Delhi HC Restrains RSY News
meta_description: Delhi High Court permanently restrains RSY News after finding most disputed uploads copied ANI's videos wholesale as a substitute for the original.
card_tip: Before reusing a rival's footage under the reporting-current-events exception, add independent reporting of your own; reproducing the original wholesale will not qualify as fair dealing.

case_name: Sun Pharma Laboratories Ltd. v. Finecure Pharmaceuticals Ltd. & Ors.
citation: FAO(OS)(COMM), decided 1 July 2026
holding_summary: Sun Pharma has sold its acid-reflux drug under the mark Pantocid since 1999, and it says it can prove continuous use with invoices going back that far. When Finecure Pharmaceuticals began selling Pantopacid, along with Pantopacid D and Pantopacid SR, Sun Pharma sued for trademark infringement, arguing that a patient reading a prescription or a chemist pulling a strip off the shelf could easily mix up two pantoprazole-based drugs with names this close. The Single Judge, Justice C. Hari Shankar, did not see it that way back in 2023, and refused Sun Pharma interim relief. His reasons were not about the marks' similarity as such but about Sun Pharma's own conduct and the strength of its registration: he found a credible challenge to the validity of the Pantocid registration, pointed to what he regarded as suppression of material facts by Sun Pharma in presenting its case, and noted an unexplained delay before Sun Pharma moved the Court at all. On that combination, interim injunction was refused, notwithstanding a prima facie finding of infringement. Sun Pharma appealed, and the Division Bench of Justice V. Kameswar Rao and Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora set the Single Judge's order aside. Their central objection was not that the Single Judge got the facts wrong but that he approached the legal starting point incorrectly. Under Section 31(1) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, registration itself carries a presumption of prima facie validity; a defendant who wants to resist an injunction by attacking that validity has to do more than raise a credible doubt, because the statute puts its thumb on the scale in favour of the registered proprietor at the interim stage. The Bench held that the Single Judge had not properly given Sun Pharma's registration the benefit of that presumption before weighing it against the suppression and delay arguments.
why_it_matters: Pharmaceutical companies frequently defend against trademark infringement suits by attacking the validity of a rival's registration, hoping to avoid interim injunction while that challenge plays out; this ruling confirms a single judge cannot treat such a challenge as neutralising the registration's statutory presumption of validity without clearing a higher bar. Defendants relying on validity challenges alone, without displacing that presumption, should expect interim relief to go against them on appeal.
title: Division Bench Overturns Refusal of Injunction, Restrains Finecure's 'Pantopacid' Over Sun Pharma's 'Pantocid'
meta_description: Delhi High Court Division Bench reverses a single judge for discounting the presumption of validity attached to Sun Pharma's registered 'Pantocid' mark.
card_tip: A validity challenge to a rival's registered mark must displace the Section 31(1) presumption of validity, not just raise doubt about it, to defeat an interim injunction application.

case_name: Angurbala Mondal v. State of West Bengal & Ors.
citation: W.P.A. 22494 of 2026, 2026 LiveLaw (Cal) 393, decided 14 September 2026
holding_summary: Angurbala Mondal had a complaint familiar to anyone who has ever lived next to someone else's livestock operation: she said two neighbouring dairy units were running without proper authorisation and that their effluent, waste and general operation posed a serious health hazard to her and the rest of the area. She wanted the local police to step in and shut the units down, and when that did not happen to her satisfaction, she took the matter to the Calcutta High Court by way of a writ petition. The State's response raised a point that recurs often across nuisance and pollution complaints against small agricultural and livestock units: the police are not equipped, and were never given the legal mandate, to measure whether a dairy operation's waste disposal, effluent discharge or general hygiene standards cross a regulatory line. That is fundamentally a technical and statutory determination, not a simple law-and-order one that a beat constable can resolve on the spot. The State also pointed out, not without some force, that Mondal herself ran a dairy farm of her own, a fact the Court noted without treating it as decisive either way on the underlying complaint. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya accepted the State's framing of the problem in full. Police officers, he held, have neither the technical expertise nor the statutory authority to adjudicate whether a dairy unit's day-to-day operations comply with environmental or health regulations, or whether they amount to a hazard serious enough to justify closure. Those are questions for a specialised regulatory body equipped to test effluent, assess waste management practices and apply the specific standards that govern livestock and dairy operations, not for a police station working off a neighbour's complaint and a site visit.
why_it_matters: Complaints against dairy and poultry units over nuisance, effluent or health hazards are common, and operators and complainants alike often look first to the police for a quick resolution; this ruling confirms that route is legally unavailable and that only the State Pollution Control Board can determine whether such an operation's practices actually violate environmental or health standards. Agricultural and dairy businesses facing police pressure over such complaints now have a clear basis to insist the matter go through the proper regulatory channel instead.
title: Police Cannot Decide If a Neighbour's Dairy Farm Is Illegal or a Health Hazard: Calcutta HC
meta_description: Calcutta High Court holds police cannot decide if a dairy farm is unlawful or a health hazard, directing the complainant to the Pollution Control Board.
card_tip: Facing police pressure over your dairy or livestock operation's waste practices, insist the complaint go to the State Pollution Control Board; police have no authority here.

case_name: Shamshid Ahmed & Ors. v. Union Territory, Chandigarh & Ors.
citation: CWP (number not available in reporting reviewed), decided on or about 24 September 2026
holding_summary: Shamshid Ahmed and fourteen others had been running a fish and poultry business on land in Mani Majra, on Chandigarh's periphery, for anywhere between twenty and thirty years by their own account. They said they had bought the land, built their sheds on it, and built a livelihood around it long before anyone questioned whether the structures belonged there. On 13 April 2026, the authorities issued an order for their demolition under the Punjab New Capital (Periphery) Control Act, 1952, the law that has governed unplanned construction around Chandigarh since the 1950s precisely to stop this kind of haphazard growth from swallowing the city's periphery. The petitioners went to the Punjab and Haryana High Court to stop the demolition, and their strongest argument was not really about the Act's technical requirements at all. They leaned on Article 21 of the Constitution, arguing that tearing down the sheds that housed their fish and poultry operation would strip them of the livelihood they and their families had depended on for decades, and that the right to life under Article 21 has long been read to include a right to livelihood. They also argued that the demolition order ignored documents they had placed on record, denied them a fair hearing, and that in any event the authorities owed them a rehabilitation policy given how long they had occupied and worked the land. A Division Bench of Justices Jasgurpreet Singh Puri and Pravindra Singh Chauhan was not moved. The right to livelihood under Article 21 protects a person's ability to earn a living through lawful means; it was never meant to convert an illegal activity, simply by virtue of having gone on long enough to become someone's livelihood, into a legal one. Accepting the petitioners' argument, the Bench reasoned, would hand every long-running illegal occupant of controlled land a ready-made defence: point to the years spent earning a living off the illegal structure, and use that history itself as the shield against enforcement. That would make the Periphery Control Act's entire regulatory scheme redundant, since nothing stops an illegal occupant from simply waiting long enough to acquire a livelihood-based immunity from the law meant to remove them.
why_it_matters: Fish, poultry and dairy operators running informally on land around planned cities or in controlled periphery zones often assume that decades of operation and investment will count for something against a demolition order; this ruling confirms courts will not treat an Article 21 livelihood claim as a defence to illegal construction, however long-established the business. Operators in this position need to pursue regularisation or rehabilitation through policy channels proactively, rather than count on a livelihood argument to stop enforcement after the fact.
title: Right to Livelihood Cannot Shield an Illegal Fish and Poultry Shed: Punjab & Haryana HC Upholds Demolition
meta_description: Punjab and Haryana High Court upholds demolition of fish and poultry sheds in Chandigarh's periphery, holding livelihood rights cannot legalise it.
card_tip: Do not rely on years of running a livelihood business on unauthorised land as a defence to demolition; Article 21 protects earning a living lawfully, not an illegal structure that funds it.

case_name: Eco Green Buildtech Ltd. v. Vikartan Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
citation: OMP (ENF.) (COMM.) 193/2023 & EX.APPL. (OS) 1449/2023, CNR No. DLHC010405902023, decided 10 September 2026
holding_summary: Eco Green Buildtech hired Vikartan Infrastructure to build the Sikka Kamya Greens project in Greater Noida under a contract worth Rs 53.73 crore, due for completion by February 2019. It did not finish on time, and the two sides blamed each other for why. Vikartan said Eco Green had defaulted on payments and thrown up hindrances that made timely completion impossible; Eco Green said Vikartan had simply abandoned the work. A memorandum of understanding the parties signed to sort things out did not resolve matters, and in 2020 the dispute went to arbitration. Midway through the arbitration, the tribunal tried its hand at conciliation between the parties, a common enough practice where an arbitral tribunal encourages settlement talks before pressing on with a full hearing on the merits. During those talks, a procedural order came to record that Eco Green was broadly satisfied with a Local Commissioner's report on the state of the construction, and that both sides were hopeful of reaching a settlement. The optimism did not last. Conciliation failed, and the tribunal went back to deciding the arbitration on its merits, delivering an award on 28 February 2023 and a further award on 27 March 2023. The problem, as Eco Green argued when it challenged both awards under Section 34, was what the tribunal did next. Rather than starting the merits determination fresh, the tribunal relied on the earlier recorded satisfaction with the Local Commissioner's report, material that had surfaced only in the course of the failed conciliation, to decide disputed questions in the arbitration itself. Several damages findings in the awards traced back to that recorded conciliation-stage satisfaction, including a Rs 2.84 crore award for additional overheads that the Court later found had no independent evidentiary support beyond this.
why_it_matters: Arbitral tribunals that attempt conciliation mid-proceeding risk tainting the eventual award if settlement-stage material finds its way into the merits decision once talks fail, and this ruling confirms such reliance is a Section 34 ground that can take down the entire award, not just the affected findings. Parties should resist tribunal pressure to let settlement discussions blend into the arbitration record, and should object immediately if a tribunal's award appears to draw on anything said during failed conciliation.
title: Tribunal Cannot Use What a Party Said During Failed Conciliation to Decide the Same Dispute in Arbitration: Delhi HC
meta_description: Delhi High Court sets aside two arbitral awards after finding the tribunal relied on material from failed conciliation, breaching confidentiality.
card_tip: If a tribunal's award relies on anything said or conceded during failed conciliation within the arbitration, raise it as a confidentiality-based Section 34 ground; it can void the award entirely.

case_name: Bhawani Construction Pvt. Ltd. v. Odisha Real Estate Regulatory Authority
citation: OREAT Appeal No. 22 of 2026, 2026 LLBiz REAT (OD) 45, order dated 12 June 2026
holding_summary: The Odisha Real Estate Regulatory Authority opened suo motu proceedings against Bhawani Construction Pvt. Ltd., a developer, and when the company did not show up to answer the allegations, ORERA pressed ahead without it. By an order dated 14 July 2023, it imposed a penalty of Rs 7 lakh on the company for whatever regulatory default the suo motu proceedings had identified. Bhawani Construction appealed to the Odisha Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, and its central argument had nothing to do with the merits of what it had or had not done wrong. It said it never received the notice that started the whole proceeding. ORERA had sent its notice to "Plot No. 59/C, Jayadurga Nagar, Bhubaneswar, Khurda", an address the company said was never its own, at any point. It had not moved there, registered there, or operated from there. The company only learned of the ex parte penalty after the fact, by which time the proceeding had already run its full course without a single submission from the very party it was penalising. Before the Tribunal, ORERA did not try to defend the address or argue that the company had somehow dodged valid service. It fairly submitted that notice had been issued to the wrong address, a concession that settled the factual dispute at the outset and left the Tribunal to work out only what followed from it.
why_it_matters: RERA authorities across states issue a high volume of suo motu and ex parte orders against developers who do not appear, often without close scrutiny of whether notice actually reached the right address; this ruling confirms that an ex parte penalty built on defective service is void for breach of natural justice regardless of the underlying merits. Developers hit with an ex parte RERA order they never responded to should first check whether notice was correctly addressed before assuming the penalty must be challenged on substance alone.
title: Odisha REAT Sets Aside ₹7 Lakh RERA Penalty Issued Ex Parte Over a Notice Sent to the Wrong Address
meta_description: Odisha Real Estate Appellate Tribunal quashes a ₹7 lakh penalty, holding ORERA's ex parte order breached natural justice over a wrong-address notice.
card_tip: Before accepting an ex parte RERA penalty as final, verify notice went to your actual registered or operating address; defective service can void the order for breach of natural justice.

case_name: NHPC Ltd. v. BGS-SGS-SOMA (JV)
citation: Arbitral award dated 1 September 2026 (ad hoc arbitration, Lot SSL-1, Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project)
holding_summary: An arbitral tribunal ruled on a dispute between NHPC Ltd. and its civil works contractor, the BGS-SGS-SOMA joint venture, over Lot SSL-1 of the Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project, covering the diversion tunnels, coffer dams, the concrete gravity dam, the plunge pool and the cut-off wall. Against the JV's claim of roughly Rs 796.87 crore plus EUR 28.76 lakh, the tribunal awarded NHPC's contractor Rs 392.31 crore plus EUR 15.36 lakh, about 49% of what was claimed, with 10% annual interest. NHPC disclosed the award to the stock exchanges on 2 September 2026.
why_it_matters: NHPC has stated that the awarded sum qualifies as an allowable project cost that can be passed through to consumers via tariffs under the CERC Tariff Regulations, 2024, so the outcome of this contractor dispute will feed directly into the tariff the project eventually charges; it is a concrete illustration of how arbitral awards on hydro/infrastructure EPC disputes translate into regulated tariff pass-throughs rather than being absorbed solely by the generating company.

case_name: Rensar Infra Private Limited v. Rais Kasam Shaikh & Ors.
citation: Arbitration Application No. 205 of 2026; 2026 LLBiz HC(BOM) 550, Bombay High Court, order dated 7 October 2026
holding_summary: The flat buyers had approached MahaRERA under Section 18 of the RERA Act over a flat held under a December 2020 agreement for sale, and MahaRERA allowed their complaint on 14 August 2024; the promoter then invoked the agreement's arbitration clause under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Justice Amit Borkar declined to treat every promoter-allottee dispute under RERA as non-arbitrable as a class, and instead referred to a larger bench the question whether the conclusion in paragraph 63(i) of Rashmi Realty Builders Pvt. Ltd. v. Rahul Rajendrakumar Pagariya (2024 SCC OnLine Bom 3871) states a general rule of non-arbitrability, given the contrary reasoning in Abhay Damodar Kanhere v. Morya Infraconstruct. The Court also declined to reject the buyers' compensation claim at the Section 11 stage itself.
why_it_matters: Puts a widely-cited 2024 ruling that had been read as making all promoter-allottee RERA disputes non-arbitrable back under review, so developers and allottees litigating under an agreement for sale with an arbitration clause should watch for the larger bench's answer before assuming either forum is settled.

case_name: M/s Sharma Enterprises v. National Building Construction Corporation (NBCC)
citation: 2026 INSC 1135; Civil Appeal No. 13782 of 2026, Supreme Court, decided 15 October 2026
holding_summary: Clause 26 of the Special Conditions of Contract between the contractor and NBCC provided for running bills and separately barred interest claims tied to withheld deposits or delayed monthly/final payments, 'or otherwise'. A Single Judge of the Delhi High Court had upheld the arbitrator's substantive award but set aside the pre-reference and pendente lite interest component as contrary to Clause 26, and a Division Bench dismissed the contractor's further appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the contractor's appeal, holding that 'or otherwise' is residuary wording of wide scope consciously used to cover every other circumstance in which interest might be claimed, following its earlier rulings in Sayeed Ahmed and Jaiprakash Associates on similarly worded clauses, and that an arbitrator exceeds jurisdiction under Section 31(7)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 by awarding interest a contract expressly bars. The underlying monetary award and post-award interest under Section 31(7)(b) were left undisturbed.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a residuary phrase like 'or otherwise' in a contractual interest-bar clause will be read as a comprehensive bar rather than limited to the specific situations listed alongside it, so parties drafting or resisting such clauses should expect courts to give the residuary words their full, independent effect rather than reading them down by association with the preceding list.

case_name: Tata Capital Limited v. Sanjay Mahajan
citation: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1067 of 2026, NCLAT (Delhi), order dated on or about 6 October 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), Delhi
holding_summary: Tata Capital, a secured creditor of the corporate debtor in liquidation, had filed its claim in Form D on 1 October 2024 entering 'NIL' for security details and 'No' on whether the security had been relinquished, then participated in Stakeholders' Consultation Committee meetings, and only about six months later sent an email purporting to elect to realise its security outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 of the IBC. NCLT Mumbai refused to exclude the hypothecated assets from the liquidation estate, also rejecting Tata Capital's argument that a pending Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 should extend the statutory window for making that election. NCLAT dismissed Tata Capital's appeal, holding the Form D entries and conduct did not clearly communicate an election to stand outside the liquidation estate within the time allowed, that a secured creditor cannot simultaneously participate in liquidation while keeping open the option to withdraw its security depending on the outcome of a later scheme, and that the belated email could not cure the earlier non-compliance.
why_it_matters: A secured financial creditor must make an unambiguous, timely election under Section 52 to stand outside the liquidation estate, and cannot hedge by filing an ambiguous Form D, participating in the SCC, and only later asserting the election once a parallel scheme's outcome becomes relevant to its interests.

case_name: NCLAT re: separate CIRP against Earth Towne Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (ETIPL)
citation: NCLAT, New Delhi, order reported 8-12 October 2026 (Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan and Technical Member Naresh Salecha)
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), New Delhi
holding_summary: Earth Towne Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (ETIPL) was a special-purpose company formed on land leased by the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), of which Earth Infrastructures Ltd. (EIL) later acquired 98% and exclusive development rights; EIL's own CIRP began in 2018, and after NCLAT had set aside NCLT's 2021 approval of the Roma Unicon Designex Consortium's resolution plan for EIL, the Supreme Court restored that plan on 5 May 2026 in Alpha Corp Development Pvt. Ltd. v. GNIDA & Ors., lifting the corporate veil between EIL and land-holding subsidiaries including ETIPL. A separate roughly Rs. 28.64 crore CIRP had nonetheless been admitted against ETIPL itself. NCLAT set aside that separate CIRP, holding there was no default by ETIPL distinct from the claims already resolved under the restored EIL plan, and that allowing a fresh, separate process would resurrect the very corporate separateness the Supreme Court had already disregarded.
why_it_matters: Where the Supreme Court has lifted the corporate veil between a parent undertaking in CIRP and a land-holding special-purpose subsidiary to restore a single resolution plan, a creditor cannot revive a parallel insolvency process against that subsidiary on claims the restored plan already covers — relevant to the roughly 4,200 homebuyers whose flats depend on the EIL plan's finality.

case_name: Ebix Cash World Money / Ebix Technologies v. Amadeus IT Group SA
citation: Delhi High Court judgment dated 1 July 2026; SLP against it dismissed by the Supreme Court (Diary No., bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana)
court: Delhi High Court (enforcement order), Supreme Court (dismissed Ebix's SLP)
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court (Justice Jasmeet Singh) held an ICC arbitral award in favour of the Spanish travel-technology company Amadeus IT Group enforceable in India to the extent of the outstanding EUR 9.71 million (around Rs. 104.55 crore), rejecting Ebix's objections on limitation, public policy and force majeure. On limitation, the Court held there is 'no straight jacket formula' for when the right to apply for enforcement accrues, and that in this case it ran from the date the award was communicated, not from the date of the underlying default. On public policy, it rejected Ebix's argument that the transaction was impermissible debt-factoring. The Supreme Court subsequently declined to interfere with the High Court's judgment, finding no ground to disturb it.
why_it_matters: Confirms that limitation for enforcing a foreign award in India is assessed flexibly by reference to when the award was communicated rather than a fixed limitation trigger, and that a factoring-style commercial arrangement does not by itself breach Indian public policy at the enforcement stage — both narrow the grounds available to award-debtors resisting enforcement of large foreign arbitral awards.

case_name: TV Today Network Ltd. v. Saurashtra Aaj Tak (Gujarati newspaper)
citation: Delhi High Court judgment dated 30 July 2026; Supreme Court subsequently declined to interfere (bench led by CJI Surya Kant)
court: Delhi High Court (Supreme Court declined to interfere with its order)
holding_summary: In a passing-off and trademark suit first filed in 2003 and for decades limited at the trial-court stage to permitting the Rajkot-based Gujarati newspaper to continue using 'Saurashtra Aaj Tak' alongside a disclaimer, the Delhi High Court held TV Today Network to be the prior user of the 'Aaj Tak' mark, declared 'Aaj Tak' a well-known trademark, and granted a permanent and mandatory injunction directing the newspaper to stop using 'Aaj Tak' in its name. The Supreme Court declined to interfere with that order on the newspaper's appeal, while giving it three months to comply and change its name; the newspaper had argued TV Today had not placed documentary evidence of its own trademark use or licence agreement on record, but the Court found no ground to disturb the High Court's findings.
why_it_matters: Reaffirms that a long-standing disclaimer-based coexistence arrangement does not harden into a permanent right to use a confusingly similar name, and that a mark's well-known status and a plaintiff's prior use can still be established and enforced even decades into litigation, with the disclaimer route treated only as interim relief rather than a final resolution.
